#9937. Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

As artificial intelligence squeezes early-career learning opportunities, capture-the-flag contests could be one way to help pick up the slack.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may be gobbling up entry-level jobs and learning opportunities for security practitioners, but it can't erase the value of hands-on experience with enterprise systems and security tools.

No matter how much agentic action cybersecurity teams embed into their security operations center (SOC) and the rest of their programs, smart people have to backstop that work. And the only way these "humans-in-the-loop" can do that capably is if they build up the kind of judgment that's best learned from the school of hard knocks.

The problem? With SOC tier 1 analysts becoming an endangered species and bug bounty programs on the ropes from a glut of AI submissions, the chances are dwindling for security newbies to rack up real-world experience.

There's no great fix to this career pipeline problem just yet, but some of the answers might be found in one of the industry's age-old mechanisms for both camaraderie and skill-building: the trusty capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

"CTFs give passionate talent the opportunity to grow and learn in ways that they might not have at their day jobs," says Jason Walker, a security engineer by day at software-as-a-service firm Five9. An avid CTF competitor, he won the Sentinels League competition sponsored and run by SentinelOne, beating two other finalists from a field of thousands of competitors worldwide. Besides street cred, Walker picked up a $5,000 prize for his efforts and a $10,000 donation in his name to his charity of choice, Trans Lifeline.

The livestreamed event offered up the spectacle and fun of an e-sports competition, but it may hold deeper clues as to how the industry can keep refreshing its talent pool in the coming years. As Walker puts it, CTFs are the ultimate way to expose both new and experienced cyber professionals to a wider range of problems and technologies.

"CTFs have helped me be a lot more versatile," he says. "If your company is running well and your program is mature, you aren't going to necessarily be firefighting new things every week. You're not going to be exposed to every new technique and threat. Doing CTF events and other hands-on training is a really important way to make sure you can stay up to date."

CTF competitions come in many shapes and sizes, but they fundamentally challenge players to find hidden pieces of data called "flags" buried inside intentionally vulnerable systems. Most fall into one of two formats: Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as Web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded per solve. Attack-defense events ask each team to defend its own vulnerable network while trying to break into everyone else's.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

The attack-defense format took shape at DEF CON's CTF, which started in 1996 and is still the event most associated with it. It has sprung forth a wellspring of CTF formats that range from grassroots industry events to big vendor-sponsored competitions like Sentinels League.

Sentinels League grew out of ThreatOps, a set of internal games SentinelOne's solutions engineers have run since 2020 to teach customers how to hunt through telemetry for hidden flags. This year's championship built on that with four games — Endpoint, Cloud, SIEM, and AI — spread across 12 weeks of qualifiers between June and October

The opening player pool of 2,236 entrants came from more than 100 countries, competing for a total prize pool of $100,000. Smaller prizes were dispensed across the qualifier and regional events, with the bigger prizes kept on reserve for the final, which was held in conjunction with SentinelOne's annual OneCon event.

Ryan O'Grady, director of SE operations at SentinelOne, says the firm invests the money in the prizes and the considerable logistics of running such a big event as a way to give back to the community, to build up expertise and exposure to its platform, and as a recruiting tool.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Whether motivated for the prizes or the training, the appetite for the event keeps growing. This year's drew enough interest that the company had to get a bigger ballroom to accommodate spectators.

Sentinels League is just one example of what a CTF looks like amid a much broader spectrum of competitions available. On CTFtime, the volunteer-run archive that tracks the hobbyist side of the scene, last year's calendar alone listed more than 200 individually organized events, with active teams from countries spanning every populated continent.

DEF CON CTF, often called the World Series of hacking, pulled 673 teams through its 2026 qualifiers before finals in Las Vegas this August. The National Cyber League, a nonprofit circuit O'Grady competes in, drew more than 7,500 students from 670 schools and universities this past spring. Kaspersky continues to run its own wildly popular SAS CTF out of Bali.

Other more academic events, such as New York University's CSAW and Carnegie Mellon's picoCTF, run versions aimed at students. Larger consulting firms, such as KPMG, use the format to scout corporate recruits.

In spite of the obvious demand for CTFs evident in the number of events held worldwide and the thousands of participants willing to sink their personal time into these pursuits, many security pundits worry about what AI is going to do to the purpose and purity of these competitions.

CTF organizers are thinking deeply about what this means for their rule books and how they enforce them. RITSEC's 2026 rules ban using AI to autonomously solve challenges outright, calling it against the spirit of the competition. Meantime, CSAW leaned into AI, this year creating an entire track built around using large language models (LLMs) to solve past CTF problems.

DEF CON CTF's 2026 qualifier split the difference. It barred fully autonomous AI teams but let human competitors use AI tools as long as a person stayed meaningfully in charge, requiring every team to label itself No AI, Low AI, or Human-Led AI on the public scoreboard.

A recent study of hundreds of Hack The Box machines released between 2017 and 2025 found solve times dropped roughly 16% a year, with the steepest declines after 2022. The hardest tier of challenges went from a 15-hour median solve down to about five, according to penetration tester Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs, who did the analysis.

He's not the only one worried. An academic study earlier this year from IBM Research and the College of William & Mary pitted 41 participants in a live, on-site CTF against four autonomous AI agents. It found that those agents placed second overall, ahead of most of the human teams competing.

Findings like these are enough to get firms like OtterSec, a blockchain security firm, to make noise about how to "save" CTFs. This summer the firm launched a $100,000 "Save CTFs Fund" to bankroll new formats that stay meaningful as AI keeps improving.

SentinelOne's O'Grady doesn't buy the death-of-CTFs talk. In his view, AI just forces organizers to redesign CTFs so they still force a human to think laterally, AI assistance or not.

AI may not be killing creative CTFs anytime soon, but it is definitely making cybersecurity's career ladder wobble. In the process it may actually be making CTFs even more crucial.

SANS Institute polled nearly 1,000 security leaders and found unclear career progression to be one of the top hiring challenges, cited by 32%, more than triple the rate last year. Only one-quarter of organizations say they have a clearly defined career path, and entry-level jobs that used to train the next generation of defenders are diminishing. SOC and security analyst roles lead the AI-driven cuts, down 32%. Threat intelligence analysts are next, at 26%, with incident responders close behind, at 22%.

Bug bounty programs are buckling under AI's pressure. At the start of the year, maintainers of the open source project Curl shut down their program after a massive influx of junk AI submissions. HackerOne paused its Internet Bug Bounty program in April after a wave of low-quality, AI-assisted reports flooded in. And this month Google Bug Hunters also paused its open source bounty program due to similar problems.

These are all blows for cyber career progression, as bug bounty problems were another great place for security professionals to flex their skills publicly and for newcomers to gain a foothold into the industry.

As long as CTF organizers can keep their competitions relevant, these events will remain a valuable puzzle piece in the skills training picture for the industry, alongside other important hands-on challenges like cyber ranges.

"With LLMs basically sweeping the table on bug bounties, it's become even harder than it already was for people to get out there, show off their skills, and get their name out there," O'Grady says. "AI has only increased the importance of CTF events like this."

#9936. How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and showed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:

Agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

Smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

What puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

"Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

No model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

We evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

The number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:

Reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:

Table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

Memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

The lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:

A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):

TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company

#9935. OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models

How much damage can a rogue agent do in 35 seconds? Asking cos that’s how long it might take to shut one down

In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior.

“As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post.

The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.”

The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster.

“The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises.

A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.”

OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one.

The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development.

“Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.”

OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.”

That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

#9934. Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series discusses some of the trends and topics from Cybersecurity Awareness Month, from using AI for better training to educating next-generation workforces on modern risks and emerging threats.

AI is changing the concept of cybersecurity awareness in more ways than one.

In the latest installment of our monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea, and Dark Reading's Rob Wright discuss some of the trends they've observed during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which has shifted during the AI era with the emergence of news threats as well as revamped defense strategies.

As we’ve seen in years past, cybersecurity awareness training often becomes a compliance checkbox exercise rather than a vehicle to educate employees and users on the latest threats. And unfortunately, the threat landscape today is changing at a frenetic pace. Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply chain compromises.

Thankfully, as the editors explain, some organizations are updating their programs to take more specific, line-of-business approaches for training while also accounting for the evolving threats related to AI; some programs are even using AI to create more convincing phishing simulations. Meanwhile, several US colleges and universities have increased their education offerings for AI security.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The editors discuss these topics and more in this Reporters' Notebook episode.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading, and welcome to another edition of the Reporter's Notebook. I am here with Sharon and Eric. Would you guys like to introduce yourselves and then we'll get into the topics for today?

There's been a lot going on, a lot of attacks, a lot of threats, a lot of urgent stuff going on in cybersecurity. But we wanted to get into some of those things here in this video discussion. Sharon, do you want to kick us off?

But it does kind of give a springboard, as we called it in one of our articles, to further focus on cybersecurity throughout the year and bring a renewed focus for this month. And one report I was reading, a SANS report, said that 19% of organizations have cybersecurity awareness training programs designed primarily to meet a specific compliance or audit requirement. And that's kind of a bad way to look at things, just doing this for compliance.

Obviously, you want to do it to be secure all the time. And, you know, we all probably groan when those awareness trainings come into our inboxes every couple months or a couple times a year. They can be boring and you just click through them just to get through them and do the checkbox. But sometimes those aren't quite as effective as they should be, as we've seen. Really, you don't want to treat it as a check space, compliance checkbox exercise.

And one major thing that we learned from our reporting, or I think we've known for years, but it's not one size fits all, right? You really want to identify the behaviors within your organization that create risk. You want to map those threats to business consequences, establish baselines, and monitor for deviations from those.

Threat s like deepfakes trying to get into your help desk and reset MFA or, you know, the common Arup example of the CFO who was on a call with an employee and wanted them to wire a ton of money to them. And you know, you really have to focus those down on what departments really need specific trainings. I guess within the organization, you have so many different types of people to cover. You have your general employees, you have C-level, privileged admins, HR recruiting, customer-facing employees, and you have third parties, contractors, and you want to match the awareness to those sorts of risks.

I guess another thing that we can talk about too is updating the program regularly. You do want to talk about older tech. We all know that phishing is a major thing, right? So make them highly relevant, personalized, and you really want to have those short, easy-to-consume bits that are good for your employees.

You have to know that a lot of the stuff that you're going to be digging up out there, if it's not through an official app store of for an official channel, it very well likely could be a scam or some type of social engineering scheme that's going to drop an infostealer or something worse on your system. So I kind of focused on preparing the next workforce to understand not only AI, but also how to guard against threats related to AI.

So I spoke to people at a number of schools that have tried to build or begin building curricula around AI security. Spoke to folks at Carnegie Mellon. For those of us who are perhaps a little pessimistic that college students want to focus on security when all the money and the attention is in building and deploying new products, I think this story that I wrote was kind of a somewhat of a corrective to that narrative, but also just as a source of optimism that at least according to the folks who are teaching this material, there are folks interested in learning about this kind of stuff and there are folks interested in pursuing graduate school education and getting certificates specifically in the security part of AI, which again is good to see. DR's Rob Wright: Thank you. Yeah, no, that's great news. it sounds like a welcome development. So maybe there is something to look forward to with AI. Fingers crossed.

#9933. Up to 3.2x Faster Inference with LFM2.5-DSpark

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:

We follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

We measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

The block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:

For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:

Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-DSpark: Up to 3.2x Faster Inference from H100 to MacBook", Liquid AI Blog, Aug 2026.

#9932. Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Obvious phishing emails with numerous red flags are somehow getting past some of the industry-leading secure email gateway (SEG) products.

Attackers are managing to sneak low-grade phishing emails through brand name email security products, as evidenced by a recent Anthropic impersonation campaign.

The campaign, described in a new blog post by Cofense, won't impress anybody. Since September, an unidentified threat actor has been sending out emails around the world, pretending to grant early access to Anthropic's cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Their goal: stealing Google and Microsoft account credentials.

To avoid being relegated to spam folders, the attacker has been using novice tactics: shortening their malicious URLs, adding CAPTCHAs to their phishing flow, and leveraging legitimate video conferencing tools. The only remarkable thing about the campaign, really, is that it actually seems to be working.

Even as far as phishing campaigns go, this one's pretty lazy.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Attackers are appealing to targets with VIP invites to a "private preview" of Anthropic's supposed "new social media AI tool." Emails emphasize that this special early look is "private, invitation-only."

Right off the bat, there are ample reasons to be suspicious. The email titles have a grammatical error. The email sender's name includes a typo — "Austin from nthropic" — and their domain belongs to GoTo Webinar, not Anthropic. Visually, the messages are barebones, possessing no visual elements that even attempt to impersonate Anthropic branding.

If for some reason someone actually clicks on the fake registration link — a link that doesn't point to an Anthropic or even a conferencing app domain — they'll end up on a fake Zoom meeting page. If, further, the victim doesn't catch that a GoTo Webinar invite led to a Zoom call, they might choose to sign into Zoom via Google or Microsoft Single-Sign On (SSO). If they choose Google, they won't even be prompted for a password, thus making half of this malicious campaign completely useless, even to the attacker running it.

Inconsistent brand impersonations and missing or broken data theft flows are endemic to AI-generated campaigns; Cofense couldn't confirm if AI was used here. "However, due to the multiple variations of Zoom pages, it's likely generative AI was used," Cofense researcher Jacob Malimban says.

He points to one bit of additional evidence: Beginning Oct. 28, the threat actor began spoofing Anthropic's website instead of Zoom's. The similar but slightly off format of the Anthropic spoofing page, he says, also suggests AI generation.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

The overall package is so maladroit that one can only wonder how such an email bypassed any spam filter in the first place. In fact, Cofense found these emails getting through market-leading email security products like the Proofpoint Secure Email Gateway (SEG) and Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Cofense pointed to a few little details that might help explain why.

First, the emails are sent from a legitimate email address, customercare@gotowebinar[.]com — a shared sender address that any GoTo Webinar user might use to distribute webinar information. The legitimacy and ubiquity of this shared address shields the sender from scrutiny.

Second, the malicious registration link in the emails was run through a URL shortener, Zapier, eliminating a security product's ability to interpret red flags in the domain itself.

Lastly, the phishing flow incorporates two separate CAPTCHAs. The first — a Cloudflare CAPTCHA, presented before the fake Zoom or Anthropic page — is meant to stop an automated scanner in its tracks.

The second CAPTCHA — placed between the fake Zoom or Anthropic page and the fake SSO page — is a malicious twist on the form, designed to block VPN services, Tor browsers, and other tools defenders might use. "Some phish kits used that specific type of CAPTCHA before. It appears to have been actively developed by threat actors to detect the tools of both automated and human activity, as well as see if the IP address was proxied," Malimban explains.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

None of these tactics will knock anyone's socks off but, in the gestalt, they seem to do the trick.

"The reality of modern cybersecurity is that Secure Email Gateways (SEGs) will always have blind spots," he says.

Barney adds that organizations should assume phishing emails will end up in employees' email inboxes, and therefore security teams need to build defenses that focus on identity.

"If an employee is tricked by a fake Anthropic lure and their Microsoft or Google credentials are compromised, strict least-privilege access policies, phishing-resistant multifactor authentication and privileged access management are what prevent the attacker from moving laterally, elevating privileges and accessing sensitive data," he advises. Lastly, he adds, "Utilizing a centralized password manager that validates domain URLs before autofilling credentials provides a critical last line of defense against the lookalike domains used in this attack, neutralizing the threat at the point of interaction."

In the spirit of Cybersecurity Awareness Month 2026, and its emphasis on avoiding and reporting phishing scams, Malimban adds, "We hope that employees are trained using Secure Behavior Management to recognize and report phishing. To defend against suspicious account access, organizations should have robust account monitoring, like with CISA's free tool (Logging Made Easy). All in all, having multiple controls and defense in depth is necessary to defend against modern attacks."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9931. UK's 'buy British' tech ambitions hit reality as less than £1 in £6 stays at home

Whitehall's biggest IT suppliers are overwhelmingly foreign, and Uncle Sam is making a killing

The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech.

A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered.

A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft.

In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending.

Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers.

And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole.

Competition is another concern. According to IPPR, 89.9 percent of government IT contracts over the past 12 months had no published record of how many suppliers bid for the work, making it difficult to assess how competitive those procurements were.

Things get murkier when AI enters the picture, naturally. Government spending records show relatively little money going directly to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, but that doesn't mean Whitehall isn't buying their technology. Much of it is bundled into existing cloud agreements, enterprise software licenses, and partnerships.

One example is NHS England's rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 505,000 staff, which IPPR says was carried out under a national licensing agreement signed in June 2023, before Copilot was even generally available.

That means AI tools can reach hundreds of thousands of public sector workers through deals negotiated before those products were on the market, potentially leaving rival suppliers without an opportunity to compete.

The report, Locked In: A Realist's Agenda for Digital Sovereignty, warns that Britain's dependence on American technology could become particularly troublesome if Washington restricts access to advanced AI systems. It points to recent US restrictions on Anthropic models and limits on early access for Britain's AI Security Institute as evidence that such concerns are no longer entirely hypothetical.

The government has already committed £500 million to a Sovereign AI Fund, but researchers reckon throwing money at homegrown technology companies won't be enough to loosen Silicon Valley's grip.

Instead, they want Whitehall to negotiate technology contracts as a single customer, make it easier to switch suppliers, and work with countries including France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea to secure access to advanced AI.

Roa Powell, senior research fellow at IPPR, said: "But we cannot do it alone, and building domestic capability can't be our only bet. The UK should be working with other middle powers, pooling our buying power to shape markets and using shared leverage to secure access to frontier AI."

Darren Jones MP, who wrote the report's foreword, made a similar argument, saying Britain should work with international allies rather than attempting to build everything itself.

"We can change how the state buys technology, back industries where the UK has a genuine opportunity to lead the world, and shape markets – but we can't go it alone. We need to join with natural allies like France, Germany, Japan and Korea and make ourselves indispensable together," he said.

Whitehall might have grand plans for digital sovereignty, but it's going to be a tough sell when so much of its technology comes from across the Atlantic. And with AI already bundled into software contracts worth billions, US tech giants aren't making it easy for the government to shop elsewhere. ®

#9930. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9929. AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM

The House of Zen's Mext team promises smarter SWAP through the power of, you'll never guess: AI

AMD's latest sales pitch: Up to 99 percent of the performance with half the DRAM, provided you're willing to buy a Mext license alongside your shiny new Epyc server.

This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter.

AMD acquired the tech from Mext back in June, and according to former CEO Gary Smerdon — now CVP of business development at AMD — the tech could cut enterprise server costs by as much as 83 percent by replacing costly RDIMMs with flash storage. Of the initial 145 systems the software has been deployed on so far, he estimates customers have already saved $5 million in avoided DRAM costs.

"Conservatively, 60, 70, even 80 or 90 percent for very large memory systems, of the cost of a server can be in memory," he explained.

Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity."

Mext technology aims to offload those infrequently accessed pages to flash. The challenge, Smerdon explains, is that while flash may be 50x cheaper per bit, 30x lower power per bit, it's also 500x slower.

This is why most folks, when provisioning VPCs or servers, generally avoid swapping out to disk wherever possible: it kills application performance and sends service level agreements out the window.

So for Mext's tech to work, it needed to ensure that any pages offloaded to storage were back in DRAM before they're needed. Kind of like running an errand in the middle of the workday – so long as you're back before your boss needs you again, they'll never know you left your desk.

The problem was that the "R" in DRAM stands for random. Predicting which pages the system was going to need at which time isn't exactly trivial. The solution? (Brace for it.)

"We realized we could use AI to monitor the system and proactively push those pages back into DRAM, so that as far as the application or the operating system knew, they were there the whole time," Smerdon said. In other words: "We transparently make flash appear as DRAM."

So, "instead of buying two terabytes of DRAM for your Epyc-based server, you could buy one terabyte of DRAM, and then the next terabyte comes with Mext."

To do this, AMD’s Mext employs a number of machine learning algorithms.

"The workhorse model is a transformer derivative model, just like ChatGPT or Claude or the other famous models, but instead of predicting, for example, in the case of text, what word is next, what we're doing is predicting what page of memory is going to be required next," Smerdon explained. So long as the pages are in DRAM before they're needed, the pages don't even need to be in the right order, he added.

Training the models to predict memory access patterns accurately presents its own challenges, which, Smerdon says, makes pre-training the models impractical.

Instead, they take a single Epyc core and train the model "in under one second," he explained. From there, the model is further refined and retrained over time until it is able to predict accurately where the pages need to be and when they need to be there.

All of this training, he emphasizes, takes place on the CPU core — no GPU required, which means essentially any Epyc customer can take advantage of the software platform.

While no GPU may be required, it's worth noting that in virtualized environments, the software requires one core per VM or VPC, so the overhead scales with virtualization. Container runtimes presumably don't suffer from this same limitation. We've reached out to AMD for clarification.

According to AMD, the technology actually works. Initially, Smerdon says, the company targeted memory-hungry applications like electronic design automation (EDA) and content creation, but later expanded to support latency-sensitive applications like databases and agentic AI pipelines.

"When pages of memory are cold, we can push them off to flash, and there's literally no impact on performance," he said.

Smerdon is overstating things just a little here. Depending on the application and how much memory is offloaded to flash, there is a performance penalty.

According to tests against Synopsys' PrimeTime EDA suite, he claims, half the memory can be offloaded to flash using Mext and the system still achieves 95 percent of the performance of DRAM. With 25 percent DRAM and 75 percent flash, performance fell to 80 percent of the DRAM-only baseline in AMD's tests.

EDA tools are extremely memory-hungry, but the amount of data the cores are working on at any given moment is often measured in megabytes. This is why AMD's Epyc X-chips remain so popular with EDA customers and why Mext targeted it initially.

In other scenarios, like Apache Spark, AMD's Mext team says it is seeing 99 percent of the performance even after replacing half the DRAM in the system with flash.

While implementing the tech may cost some performance, AMD is betting that customers will be willing to make that compromise in exchange for substantial DRAM savings, as memory remains constrained thanks to the AI datacenter buildout.

Right now, AMD is working to integrate Mext into its broader enterprise portfolio. The software, we're told, will be exclusive to AMD hardware and will be offered as a license sold through OEM partners.

Systems running Linux require only a kernel driver to take advantage of the software, while a separate RAM View application is being offered to help enterprises understand which systems and workloads it should be enabled on.

The chip designer says it's currently in the first phase of its Mext rollout, which means working with OEMs like HPE to ensure systems are so-called "Mext ready." In the second phase, the company aims to begin selling licenses for the software and shipping Epyc platforms with RAM View preinstalled.®

#9928. As Russia's Cyberwar Evolves, Belarus Steps Forward

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The "FrostyNeighbor" advanced persistent threat (APT) launched a destructive attack in Ukraine and is raising concerns about deeper alignment with Russian cyber objectives.

Researchers have spotted the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor against a critical target in Ukraine, suggesting Belarus may be upping its support for Russian national objectives — carrying implications for much of Europe.

ESET this week published its APT Activity Report for Q2 and Q3 2026. The report highlights a range of state-sponsored activity across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, but one of the most significant assertions involves Belarus, an Eastern European country that has been close allies with Russia in the latter's invasion of Ukraine.

Historically, Belarusian cyber operations have been tracked separately from those attributed directly to Russian intelligence services, though researchers have long observed overlap in targeting and strategic interests. The Belarusan state-affiliated group FrostyNeighbor — also tracked as UNC1151 — has been known for disinformation and cyber espionage, the latter conducted through various means such as spear phishing and malware.

Related:Russia's Hybrid Cyber-Physical War in Europe Heats Up

While the Eastern European country has also set its sights on Ukrainian and Polish targets in phishing attacks to further its own and possibly Russia's goals, ESET identified a recent escalation in these activities. Mainly, ESET's report notes that its researchers "identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater."

Specifically, FrostyNeighbor deployed Chisel, UltraVNC, Cobalt Strike, and a VBScript wiper via Group Policy against a manufacturing company in Ukraine that ESET said "plays an important role in the country's transportation sector," which is notable because destructive operations up until this point have been explicitly Russia-aligned.

"While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia," the report read. "We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas."

Damien Schaeffer, senior malware researcher at ESET, says that the strongest evidence for an increasing operational closeness with Russia is the number of attacks and the victimology that appears closer to and aligned with Russia's strategic priorities than Belarus's own, as well as a sophistication behind these attacks, "which seems relatively high to Belarus's potential interests alone." He says ESET first observed this trend of increasing aggressiveness at the beginning of 2024.

This comes as North Korea expands its own military cooperation with Russia in the latter's war on Ukraine, which ESET added could mean cyber activity will continue to align as well.

Russia's war on Ukraine stretches far beyond Ukraine, especially in the realm of cyber operations. Russia has grown bolder in cyberattacks particularly against European countries that support Ukraine militarily or politically, are on NATO's eastern flank, and support critical logistics hubs for aid flowing into Ukraine.

This, to varying degrees, has included Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Sweden, Czech Republic, and Germany, among others. In other words, if Russian allies are growing bolder in their cyberactivities explicitly supporting Russia, that carries consequences for all of Europe.

Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, tells Dark Reading that its evidence shows FrostyNeighbor as an actor executing sustained operations and evolving its techniques, though not necessarily an overall increase in operational scale nor shared operational command.

Recorded Future's recommendation is to explicitly track Belarus-linked clusters and correlate their infrastructure, tools, and targeting with Russian threat campaigns "while preserving attribution distinctions."

"Threat models should cover credential theft, persistent access, and the use of compromised accounts to reach additional people. Intelligence collection should include malicious login infrastructure, email exploitation, personal-account targeting, and abuse of trusted contacts, which are the access routes documented in these campaigns," Leslie says. "Defenders do not need proof of Russian tasking to prioritize an actor already targeting them."

While researchers differ on whether Belarusian activity represents deeper operational integration with Russia, they appear to agree that defenders should not dismiss Belarus-linked actors as secondary threats. As Leslie explains, CERT Polska in June 2026 identified UNC1151 as one of the most active APT groups it monitors, "observing new phishing domains almost daily in the preceding weeks."

Organizations in sectors tied to government, transportation, and defense that show support for Ukraine may increasingly encounter campaigns whose objectives align closely with Moscow's broader strategic interests.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead.

Agentic AI architecture extends microservices and cloud-native architectures with AI agents that work with context, memory, and protocols such as MCP and A2A. The article covers bounded-context integration, task-dependent coordination strategies, new security risks, and observability needs. It expects gradual adoption alongside existing architectures, with platforms absorbing common components.

Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go.

Vanessa Formicola shares how technical leaders can move beyond "wishful architecture" by practicing holistic socio-technical engineering. She discusses why engineering leaders must account for organizational maturity, reward structures, geopolitical climate, and team dynamics, framing the staff-plus role as designing the conditions for technology to thrive rather than just picking tools.

Oli Lane and Julian Wreford share how Gearset replaced guesswork in distributed asynchronous queues with OpenTelemetry tracing. They explain why traditional metrics fall short, how to implement user-centric SLOs based on latency distributions, and share practical debugging tips to help senior developers, software architects, and engineering leaders improve system reliability and team culture.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience

Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go.

Aditya Mulik is a Senior Software Engineer at Walmart Global Tech specializing in large-scale distributed systems and platform engineering, with deep expertise in deploying scalable and resilient solutions. He has led the development of microservices architectures and production LLM systems, enabling high-throughput applications serving millions of requests. He also contributes to open source.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Aditya Mulik: My topic today is, Batch Intelligence at Scale, which is, Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience. My name is Aditya Mulik. I work as a senior software engineer at Walmart Global Tech.

Like, this is something that's going to happen, and then this number of stock has to be ordered. What if we can add some real-time context to it?

That's where we came up with a multi-agent — not monolith — basically a sequential workflow of agents where this agentic flow can actually determine, like get the real-time data along with some forecasting model data as well, and get the exact accurate decision that has to be given to the store manager, where these are the number of items that they need to order. How did we do that? Basically, in the sequential agentic workflow, we added multi-agent orchestration, like one agent after another, where first agent would determine, so in this case, it gathers context from various data sources for a particular department. How much of this whole solution is going to cost to run, is what was the next question. The thing over here is the PTU problem. When the solution went to production, we had humongous amount of input and output tokens being used. Since it was a foundational model, we decided to secure 400 PTUs for that amount of scale that we need to run.
