There should not be wastage happening in a particular department. Running at this position, it doesn't make sense, if these much PTUs are going to be used. PTUs is like reserved capacity, and we have to reserve it for the entire day. Any of these vendors who are providing the PTUs, we have to take it for the entire 24 hours, and it's a monthly or yearly subscription that we have to take in. Now the problem is, this is a batch intelligence application, it's only going to run overnight. It's not going to run the entire day. We are not serving any live traffic. For us, we were being charged 400 PTUs for 24 hours, and PTUs reserve capacity for the entire day.

Our workload was nightly batch run, which was not 24 by 7. We were paying for the round the clock capacity which was being used. This was our most critical problem that we were trying to solve in a particular defined set of time, which didn't make sense because of the cost involved. We started exploring options, what are the options? Because this is a foundational model, the best part about foundational model is they are well trained, they are good for such enterprise scale applications. The next thing that came to us was, what AI model should I choose? Here as you can see, we had cheaper models where we can go with open-source models or any other models, which might introduce some latency, or they could be cheaper compared to the one which we already had, whether it's a GPT-4.1 or Gemini, and so on. Or we can just reduce the PTUs, that was another option. Or we could go with pay-as-you-go. We were debating between quality versus cost, and both were not a good option, because we needed high quality but lower cost. That was the main problem that we had to solve.

How did we do that? The decision that we made was, we went with pay-as-you-go. Now just to go with some background, the problem with PTU versus pay-as-you-go, is pay-as-you-go will come with latency issues, as I've mentioned over here, and there will be rate limiting happening. We did observe a lot of rate limit issues, but now the thing is, as I mentioned in my failures as well, we had added a retry logic. This retry logic enabled us, even if there is a rate limit, if there are any 4xx or 5xx errors, I'm just going to retry again. If I do retry again, the output will be generated again. Now, if it's a pay-as-you-go, it's still a foundational model and it still gives very accurate responses, and there was no reserved capacity as well over here. We were not paying round the clock, we were just using as much compute as we require.

The payoff, so what happened over here is, we were supposed to pay around 100k per month, now we are paying just 10k as the final usage, because even with the retries, the cost is just very low. It's just going to happen in that specific 30 minutes, or maybe the time might increase. We don't mind because the stores are already closed, this is going to be a nightly job. Then, eventually, whatever compute is being taken is going to just happen at night, even if there are retries and everything, the cost will be minimal, output will be still matching the quality that we have set, because there is schema enforcement, and all the data engineering pipelines were fixed. This was our biggest win. As I mentioned, same tokens, same model, just a pricing tier switch from PTU to pay-as-you-go, and for a drastic drop in cost. That was the big win that I wanted to mention over here.

Every failure and every fix left us with a lesson worth carrying forward. Here's what we learned, building at scale. These are some of the learnings that I'm going to mention once again. Basically, schema enforcement. Since we are retrying, everything is all planned out, but schema enforcement is not just the one thing that happens over here, basic JSON validation. There has to be semantic validation, because data, what is coming from various sources, like in the AI domain, what I've learned very well is context has to be very accurate. With the data pipelines that we have, whatever context we get, if there is even a slight mismatch, it can just return vague output. We have to make sure semantic validation is in place. Data usability, making data easy to understand and use. We need to have some observability as well. Whatever the data that is coming in, we need to see how the pipelines are running.

All those things have to be taken into consideration. Then comes the data integrity. Maintaining accuracy and consistency of data is very important, is what I've learned from this entire perspective. That's one of the key features. Second thing is data engineering limits AI quality. As I mentioned over here, data quality over here is reliable AI results, accurate and trustworthy outcomes, data rectification, fixing upstream data issues, data engineering, ensuring data quality, and flawed data. What do we mean by all of this? The entire context over here, since it was a nightly job that was being run, this had a huge emphasis on the data engineering aspects itself. Because we were getting data from various sources, there was a lot of focus that was added into this perspective, where data coming from various sources has to be verified. The amount of scripts that we created were validated with the business and the data team, with the engineering team.

We ensured that once the data is very accurate, then that context will be fed properly to the agents with a proper particular prompt, and that will generate the exact output that we are looking for. Because it's a multi-agent workflow, we have to ensure that the data that is coming from various sources has to be very accurate. That was our main goal that we learned from this entire workflow. Also, like flawed data, as I mentioned, unreliable input is also like, once the input is not proper, all the agents will react in a weird output, because it might either not match to the schema, or it might just match to the schema also, but just generate vague outputs, and that's how it would return. Building retry logic, this was one of the most important aspects that I went through. We have been very much emphasizing on this.

Retries can be a very bad loop as well, where if you don't plan it properly, it can just keep retrying, and that would just increase a lot of costs. Just because there are tokens involved over here, you have to plan it very accurately. As I mentioned in the initial flow, we used to retry it at the base, like root level, where all the agents are, like where the workflow runs. Ideally, the agentic retry should be in such a pattern where it is actually needed, whether we are getting the context from the proper data source, so that the further agents don't have to hallucinate, or there could be something that can go wrong. Retry over here, implemented from the outset, reduced unexpected failures. There's proactive system enhancement, cost saving and efficiency. It results into better user satisfaction.

The next learning perspective is observability. This is one of the key things from the entire workflow, that everyone is focused on. Traceability is important, structured logging is important, and enhanced system understanding. Because once you have tracing enabled, for us, initially, when we were having this entire workflow running, we were not able to determine, ok, what's going wrong, just because there are no proper traces set up. If you're not able to identify if the LLM is hallucinating, or if the model is just getting rate limited, all that has to be clearly available. There are tools which help us add those visibility, and then having that in place, make sure that your application is very robust, and can survive any failures to make it very resilient. That's a very important aspect that I'll mention over here. The next thing is matching infrastructure to requirements. This is the key thing that we realized, which is the infrastructure should be used for a nightly batch job.

Here, we can see that the real-time infrastructure, like if you have a real-time infrastructure where users are having conversations with the LLM, in that case, you can have an accurate set of PTUs set up, and so on. In cost effective infrastructures, you need to ensure that you don't need to actually have PTUs only allocated. Here, in our case, we were opting either for like pay-as-you-go, or you can even go with open-source models. As long as it's giving you the proper performance, the correct output, that's the ideal approach that you should be going with. The next one is, I've reached the end, which is, tomorrow at 6 a.m., a store manager will confidently adjust the inventory. They don't know about our schema validation, our loop retries, our nightly API optimizations. They don't have to as well. It's just the ultimate metric, which is the resilient engineering. That's what the perspective is.

Just to recap over here, schema is our table stakes, semantics is the real work. Focus on validation checks that go beyond basic JSON structure. Data engineering limits AI quality, so garbage in results into garbage out as well. Having retry logic is very important. If there are network timeouts, hallucinations, retry can ensure that your output is always accurate. Observability is mandatory. Tracing, logging is very important. Aditya Mulik: This is the thing that I didn't include in my presentation as well, because this was our initial workflow where we went with an MVP. Because initially, our process was to come with an MVP, how should we determine the inventory accuracy. The things that we didn't include were evals. We did work upon in an iterative fashion where we had a certain perspective, like if there is a particular department, in this case, as I mentioned about rotisserie chicken, the shelf life is about 24 hours to 48 hours, is what I know about. There should be a certain eval set for particular departments as well. What we did initially was to go with a flow where we are getting real-time data. Once we have that data coming in, then we were able to iteratively add evals and a grounding mechanism, and even governance. Because at times, they were like, we had to make sure there are pricing information and everything that should not be coming in. All that was considered in an evaluation set. That's how we had approached it. That was not one of the perspectives that I did include, because that's something that was iteratively performed.

Participant 4: You mentioned that the store manager needs to act on the recommendation, either agree or override. Is there a possibility that the store manager does not take any action? Does the recommendation become stale because the next nightly run might have different parameters, and that might be a different recommendation.

Aditya Mulik: The thing is, the store managers didn't act upon it right away. The way it was done was initially when we were in the pilot phase, this was all being validated very thoroughly. The store manager has the ability to first go because it's kind of like their day-to-day process, they have their own applications where they're verifying the inventory that's coming in. This was just as a recommendation that was initially being shared to their store manager. They were manually validating it. As this went to full production, and over the iterative process of weeks and weeks, they were able to determine that the predictions were becoming more and more accurate, because that was actually the context that they were getting. The only thing was there was always a human in the loop perspective over here. Because even if the recommendation has come in, they won't just take the action right away, they will verify the inventory and then only they'll take a call. That's how it was done. It's not that they always acted upon it.

Participant 5: You mentioned the cost aspect. How did business decide in the end, is it worthwhile, given the cost to roll it out globally, or is there a tradeoff to take into account?

Aditya Mulik: This was an initial POC that we started off with. The way it was working out was initially recommendations were just based on machine learning models themselves. That's how it was running from a longer time. As this agentic workflow started coming through, and then we did already have something which was planned out to have this rolled out, like to certain pilot stores. The plan was initially to see how this fits in the entire ecosystem, because we didn't want to disturb the existing flow, because as the stores are operating right now, they're well efficient. This is just an additional layer that we added over here, just to make sure like, ok, this is getting more accurate recommendations. Then it went out as a POC, POC to the entire production, like 4700 stores. Then it was foolproof as a concept that got deployed. We iteratively kept adding more and more recommendations. Our initial plan was to do it for a specific department itself. Then that's how we scaled it up.

#9926. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

#9925. Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens

Anything Windows can bork, the penguin can bork sideways

UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better.

Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem.

There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd, an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT. Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear.

Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands.

The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery.

Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware."

Readers might be interested to know that Heathrow has spent years working on its new screens. The product owner again: "We've completely re-engineered our content distribution system to be flexible and device-agnostic."

So Windows in one place, and Linux somewhere else. All rubbing along famously. Assuming, of course, the displays can show more than a virtual cough and splutter during boot. ®

#9924. Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

A security firm patched a decade-old app to prevent the takeover of millions of machines, highlighting that abandoned domains remain a boon to attackers.

When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

#9923. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

The fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇

#9922. Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python

Newly open sourced XSE handles six million queries a second across services including Search, Ads, and YouTube Shorts

"Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work.

Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors.

The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE, short for the XLA Serving Engine.

XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google.

"LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach, Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday.

At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search.

These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing.

A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory.

In this setup, the ML boffins write their model code in Python, using Google's JAX to help with the sums. Google also plans integration with TorchTPU so PyTorch users can export models for C++ serving on TPUs. An export tool packages the model's computations in StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, alongside its trained weights in an "XLA SavedModel."

Ready to precognate, the C++ serving runtime uses XLA to compile those computations into native code for the target silicon. No Python interpreter to see here.

XLA SavedModels can run on GPUs and CPUs – Google partnered with both Arm and Intel to develop the XLA ecosystem. But Google obviously thinks it'd be a lot cooler if you ran your models on its own line of TPU accelerators.

Python's sluggishness continues to be an issue for the ML community. Beyond XSE, other approaches have been taken, many of which involve jettisoning the Python code as quickly as possible. PyTorch offers a native C++ runtime called LibTorch. Also, Microsoft and its collaborators offer the ONNX Runtime, which supports an open graph format with Python bindings.

Even Python's own reference implementation relies heavily on C, with Rust now getting a foot in the door. ®

#9921. L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

I ricercatori non riescono a spiegare del tutto perché le minacce informatiche in Italia siano così diverse rispetto a quelle di qualsiasi altro Paese.

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

Secondo nuovi dati, l’Italia è vittima di un numero sproporzionatamente elevato di attacchi informatici. Non solo: le tipologie di attacchi che colpiscono le organizzazioni nel Paese sono molto diverse da quelle che colpiscono altre località. I ricercatori avanzano tre teorie per spiegarne il motivo.

È vero che alcune regioni e alcuni paesi sono esposti a un rischio informatico maggiore a causa di fattori economici, militari e politici. Israele è una calamita per gli hacktivisti e per le minacce persistenti avanzate (APT) regionali, legate agli Stati. La storia unica del Brasile lo rende un vero e proprio alveare di trojan bancari. L’economia degli Stati Uniti attirerà sempre la massima attenzione da parte dei truffatori. Non è però così ovvio il motivo per cui l’Italia sia un bersaglio così popolare per i criminali informatici.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

«Uno dei motivi principali per cui abbiamo deciso di esaminare il panorama delle minacce in Italia è che il Paese continuava a comparire in cima alle nostre statistiche nei rapporti interni mensili», afferma Gianluca Tiepolo, analista di criminalità informatica presso Intel471. In un rapporto condiviso in esclusiva con Dark Reading prima della sua pubblicazione, Intel471 ha rilevato che l’Italia rappresenta un vero e proprio caso a sé stante nel panorama globale delle minacce informatiche. Le organizzazioni italiane subiscono attacchi a un ritmo ben superiore a quanto ci si potrebbe ragionevolmente aspettare, considerando le dimensioni del Paese, la sua economia e la sua situazione politica. Inoltre, gli attacchi sfruttanti le vulnerabilità e le infrastrutture web sono molto più comuni in Italia che altrove.

«Volevamo capire cosa fosse alla base di quelle statistiche», afferma Tiepolo. Alla fine, però, i dati dipingono un quadro quasi inspiegabile di ciò che sta accadendo nella terra della pasta e del Chianti.

L’Italia è il 25° Paese più grande al mondo ma, secondo questi nuovi dati, le sue organizzazioni rappresentano circa il 7% di tutti i dati di accesso iniziale venduti sui forum dei criminali informatici. A livello globale, è seconda solo agli Stati Uniti (30%). L’Italia si colloca inoltre al quarto posto tra i Paesi più presi di mira dal ransomware.

Ancora più strani sono i tipi di intrusioni informatiche che colpiscono le organizzazioni in Italia. Secondo i nuovi dati, gli initial access broker (IAB) hanno ottenuto il loro primo punto d’appoggio sfruttando vulnerabilità nel 57% dei casi. Le credenziali hanno spiegato solo il 23% dei casi. Nel frattempo, gli IAB hanno venduto l’accesso all’infrastruttura web di proprietà delle vittime nel 49% dei casi, con strumenti di accesso remoto e desktop remoto che rappresentano il 26% dei casi.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

E allora? Forse queste cifre non saltano all’occhio. Ora, però, confrontiamole con i dati di Intel471 tratti dal suo rapporto “2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook”:

A livello globale nel 2025, gli IAB hanno preso di mira gli strumenti di accesso remoto e di desktop remoto nel 67% dei casi — il 41% in più, in termini relativi, rispetto all’Italia. Nel frattempo, l’infrastruttura web — di gran lunga la risorsa più a rischio in Italia — rappresentava una frazione talmente esigua dei dati globali di Intel471 che l’azienda non si è nemmeno preoccupata di citarla nel proprio rapporto.

Allo stesso modo, secondo i dati globali dell’azienda, gli attacchi basati sulle credenziali sono oggi, in generale, otto volte più comuni di qualsiasi altro tipo di attacco. È emerso che il 49% delle inserzioni su IAB indicava le credenziali come tipo di attacco, rispetto al 23% dei dati specifici per l’Italia. E, cosa davvero esilarante, mentre in Italia rappresentano circa il 57% di tutti gli attacchi, le vulnerabilità sfruttate sono emerse solo nel 6,5% dei casi a livello globale.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Sebbene i dati sulla sicurezza informatica possano essere interpretati in modi diversi a seconda delle circostanze, l’Italia sembra davvero una sorta di “unicorno” del rischio informatico, afferma Tiepolo, aggiungendo che l’Italia è ormai da tempo in ritardo in termini di preparazione informatica.

«Sono italiano», dice. «Ho lavorato con molti clienti italiani diversi. Quello che posso dire è che l’Italia è probabilmente leggermente indietro rispetto ad altri paesi europei, semplicemente in termini di [adozione delle] tecnologie di sicurezza. Ad esempio, le tecnologie di rilevamento e risposta sugli endpoint (EDR) sono diventate popolari in Italia intorno al 2020–2021. Prima del 2020, la maggior parte delle aziende italiane non utilizzava la tecnologia EDR. Quindi, forse storicamente, l’Italia è un po’ indietro nell’investire effettivamente in prodotti e tecnologie di sicurezza informatica».

Inoltre, i criminali informatici opportunisti stanno sfruttando in massa vulnerabilità note, diffuse e spesso piuttosto datate per mietere un numero maggiore di vittime in Italia rispetto ad altri paesi. «I dati che abbiamo visto la scorsa settimana da PHP2Shell, credo, confermano questa valutazione. L’Italia è il paese europeo con il maggior numero di versioni PHP 4, 5 e 7, che sono ormai fuori supporto», osserva Tiepolo.

«Ben il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale rivolte all’Italia sono quelle che chiamiamo “offerte all’ingrosso”», ipotizza. «Non si tratta di offerte mirate specificatamente all’Italia, ma semplicemente di sfruttamento delle vulnerabilità. La nostra valutazione è che l’Italia sia probabilmente più lenta di altri paesi nell’applicare le patch ai propri sistemi».

Un’altra possibilità correlata è che l’Italia si trovi vittima di una sorta di effetto rete delle vulnerabilità informatiche. La logica è più o meno questa: se determinate tecnologie sono particolarmente diffuse in un paese come l’Italia e le organizzazioni sono lente nell’affrontare le vulnerabilità di tali tecnologie, allora quel paese diventa un’economia di scala attraente.

Come ha scritto Intel471 nel proprio rapporto: «Una volta che un attore sviluppa un metodo di sfruttamento efficace, può applicare tale metodo ad altri sistemi esposti senza dover condurre un’attività di ricognizione separata ed estesa contro ciascuna organizzazione. Ciò riduce lo sforzo necessario per compromettere aziende la cui dimensione o il cui profilo potrebbero altrimenti offrire un incentivo limitato per un’intrusione mirata».

I ricercatori non hanno potuto specificare esattamente a quali tecnologie, vulnerabilità o metodi di sfruttamento questa teoria possa riferirsi, ma hanno osservato che essa si inserisce nel dato secondo cui il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale alle organizzazioni italiane online viene venduto all’ingrosso.

Senza avallare specificatamente i dati o le conclusioni di Intel471, i rappresentanti della società di sicurezza informatica Cleafy, con sede a Milano, hanno dichiarato a Dark Reading di aver osservato modelli sostanzialmente simili.

«La nostra ricerca sulle minacce evidenzia effettivamente un modello correlato: gli autori degli attacchi riutilizzano strumenti, infrastrutture e tecniche per estendere le campagne a diversi obiettivi bancari italiani», ha scritto l’azienda via e-mail. Ha citato casi come il kit di iniezione web drIBAN, che gli autori degli attacchi hanno utilizzato per sfruttare il sistema di Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC), ampiamente diffuso in Italia. Casi come quello di drIBAN «non dimostrano che l’Italia abbia un mercato di accesso iniziale sproporzionatamente ampio, ma illustrano come le tecniche di attacco e le infrastrutture riutilizzabili possano aiutare i criminali informatici a estendere le operazioni su più obiettivi».

C’è un altro fattore, potenzialmente significativo, che spiega perché l’Italia appaia così diversa dagli altri paesi nei set di dati sugli attacchi informatici: la prevalenza delle piccole imprese.

La maggior parte delle imprese, ovunque, è di piccole dimensioni, ma, almeno rispetto ad altre economie avanzate, ciò è particolarmente vero in Italia. Una “panoramica dei dati per l’Italia” del maggio 2024 redatta da McKinsey ha rilevato che le “MSME” — micro, piccole e medie imprese — hanno contribuito all’economia e all’occupazione italiane in misura superiore di circa il 10% rispetto alla loro quota relativa in altre economie avanzate. Lo scorso marzo, inoltre, l’Organizzazione per la cooperazione e lo sviluppo economico (OCSE) ha pubblicato un rapporto in cui si indicava che nel 2023 il 99,9% delle imprese italiane era costituito da PMI e il 94,8% da microimprese.

«L’Italia ha molte piccole e medie imprese», afferma Tiepolo. «Una delle cose emerse dai dati — in particolare quelli relativi alle estorsioni — è che questi gruppi prendono di mira [in modo sproporzionato] le piccole e medie imprese. Quindi questo potrebbe essere uno dei motivi per cui [l’Italia si distingue] rispetto ad altri paesi che hanno un maggior numero di grandi aziende».

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9920. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

#9919. Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

A recent law enforcement operation to dismantle harmful scam centers was a big success. A threat intelligence expert walks us through what happened and why he wants more of the same.

Pushes for public-private partnerships to address escalating cyber threats have been on the industry's radar for years. Collaboration has been a focal point in cybersecurity conference panels and government initiatives. Calls for more information-sharing and analysis centers have been persistent.

As director of preemptive cyberdefense at Silent Push, Michael Sweeney had a front-row seat to this kind of partnership when his company recently took part in "Operation Blackout," a coordinated international operation to take down criminal networks operating out of West Africa.

Operation Blackout coordinated efforts by the UK's National Crime Agency, the US Department of Justice (DoJ), the FBI, and private industry partners — including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Silent Push — to disrupt criminal networks behind pig-butchering, romance, and cryptocurrency scams. The DoJ announced that the campaign resulted in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and the removal of more than 3.7 million fake social media accounts.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

As the UK's main law enforcement agency, the National Crime Agency hosted Joint Disruption Week in London in early October to bring together the DoJ and the FBI with private industry partners to share real-time intelligence. In addition to US authorities and private industry partners, the Nigerian Joint Case Team on Cybercrimes, the Nigeria Police Force-National Cybercrime Center, and Ghanaian Cyber Security Authority also participated.

The Joint Disruption Week marked the first coordinated effort specifically focused on West Africa, according to the DoJ, which noted that global commitments are essential to dismantling the far-reaching scam centers.

The goal of these operations is to tackle scam activity at the global scale it has reached today, Sweeney explains. The more people who participate, the "better off we are," he says.

"The idea is not only to stop the current scams, but also to look across all of these different events," Sweeney tells Dark Reading. "[Industry and government are] all needed together in order to get this successfully taken down."

Data taken from scams reported through the FBI's Internet Complaint Center and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre formed the initial basis for Operation Blackout. From there, law enforcement compiled information, including the domains the scammers used and the infrastructure they set up to manipulate people for money.

Then the collaboration really began. Meta provided some of the data that helped drill down to specific regions — a surprising move, since social media platforms don't generally cooperate with law enforcement, despite threat actors abusing platforms to lure in victims. Several other organizations sent signals to further paint a picture of the attacker's intent and infrastructure.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Silent Push's role involved providing 35,000 domains, creating more than 70 detection rules to trigger alerts when malicious activity occurs, and fingerprinting, Sweeney says. All of those are considered the "common choke points" that help researchers and authorities map the threat actors' network patterns.

Everything was analyzed, and the data augmented each other to provide the evidence authorities needed to take down the scammers, Sweeney says.

"Once you get everyone in the room with all the data, it becomes easier to see the big picture," he says. "From that, see where the attacks are coming from, the commonalities, and who is the most important person to take down in the operation, and where you want to go to get these people."

Sweeney attributes the success of Operation Blackout and other operations he has worked on over the years to how clear the mission was; everyone was on the same page about the goals and importance of data sharing, he says. Many of the legal or jurisdiction blockers that would otherwise prevent them from sharing information and hinder actual action were removed, including data-sharing agreements with users.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

A number of providers were also involved, including Starlink. While each platform offers different services, they united in a shared stance. The camaraderie and energy that accompanied it were palpable, Sweeney says.

"We come together [to] say, 'If you're abusing our services, we're going to do everything we can to stop you, and we're going to pull in law enforcement,'" he says.

One thing Sweeney would like to change is the pace; he would like to see these partnerships move faster and conduct more operations as scammers drain billions from the US economy. Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence.

Sweeney says the people who just report a scam or who are too ashamed to come forward at all draw him to this work. They should know they aren't alone and that people are working hard to fight back, he adds.

"Everyone really wants to stop it, so pacing may be the only frustration," Sweeney says. "Let's do more. Hit them while they're down so that more people don't have that moment where they're having to figure out how to report a scam.”

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9918. Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft

Says it 'strongly' suspects attack limited to legacy system, and that nothing sensitive is at risk

Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured.

"Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said.

"The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI."

Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations.

Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available.

"Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact.

"As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact.

"Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident."

Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017.

Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy.

Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU).

Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs.

Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days.

In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®
