#9862. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9860. APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

After compromising websites, the Russian state-sponsored threat group is fingerprinting victims, then harvesting information from the interesting ones.

It has emerged this week that Russia's APT29 threat group compromised the website of a Ukrainian SEO and website analytics service, and briefly used the access to distribute malicious device-fingerprinting code to potentially thousands of iPhone and Android users.

The weeklong compromise earlier this year was part of a broader watering-hole campaign from APT29 (aka Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes) that also used other legitimate and fake websites to distribute the fingerprinting malware, and later to collect sensitive personal information from selected devices.

Researchers at Sekoia who are tracking the campaign are unsure if the state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) had specific targets in mind, or if it was simply trying to infect as many vulnerable phones as possible.

"Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis," Sekoia's threat research and intelligence team wrote. "While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation."

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

APT29 is a familiar threat actor that the US government has formally tied to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its primary mission is intelligence gathering on behalf of Moscow, with a focus on government agencies, diplomatic organizations, think tanks, technology companies, healthcare, and research institutions.

Among its most prominent campaigns were the breaches at the Democratic National Committee in 2016, efforts to steal COVID-19 vaccine research in 2020, and the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, which gave it access to numerous US government agencies and private-sector organizations. The group is known for stealthy, long-term intrusions, and in recent years has increasingly targeted cloud environments, email accounts, and technology providers to gain access to downstream victims.

In its latest campaign, APT29 used three separate infection vectors to target iOS and Android devices. One involved compromising legitimate websites and injecting malicious JavaScript that exposed visitors to a device-fingerprinting script. Among the websites the threat actor turned into watering holes were those of a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, and a Bulgarian military-related organization.

When unable to compromise a legitimate website, the group created lookalike domains that impersonated the real sites, and modified their content in real-time to inject the malicious code. Two examples it impersonated were the America250 national celebration website and London's Raffles hotel.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

The third vector involved a supply chain compromise of Ukrainian website analytics firm Plerdy. According to Sekoia, thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, use the company's tracking scripts. By injecting malicious code into that script, APT29 potentially exposed visitors to those sites to its device-fingerprinting and exploit-delivery infrastructure, Sekoia said.

The fingerprinting malware collected device and browser data from Android and iOS devices and sent it to an APT29 command-and-control service, which then delivered one of three different exploit chains depending on the mobile platform and browser/OS versions. Each chain targeted specific vulnerabilities in iOS or Android that had remained unpatched on the exposed devices.

Related:Video Call Exploit Chains Two Flaws in Unisoc Modems

Sekoia said it found several indicators linking the campaign to APT29, including remnants of a separate 2025 watering-hole operation that researchers have previously attributed to the group. Sekoia also found signs that the attackers may have obtained their exploits from a third party, possibly a commercial surveillance vendor (CSV). The campaign's victims include organizations in Europe and the US, though most are based in Ukraine, a country that Russian threat groups have incessantly targeted since the beginning of the war in Ukraine.

APT29's latest campaign is another indication of how mobile devices have become attractive intelligence targets for threat groups. Commercial spyware vendors are fueling the trend by making technology available that enables large scale surveillance and data theft via mobile devices. APT29's likely sourcing of the DarkSword exploit kit from a third-party provider suggests that sophisticated mobile intrusion capabilities that were once largely associated with highly targeted espionage operations are finding their way into broader campaigns.

"The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation," Sekoia warned. "Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Uncorking Queueing Bottlenecks with OpenTelemetry

Oli Lane and Julian Wreford share how Gearset replaced guesswork in distributed asynchronous queues with OpenTelemetry tracing. They explain why traditional metrics fall short, how to implement user-centric SLOs based on latency distributions, and share practical debugging tips to help senior developers, software architects, and engineering leaders improve system reliability and team culture.

Julian Wreford is an engineering team lead at Gearset where he leads the team responsible for all things site reliability. Oli Lane is an Engineering Team Lead at Gearset. Currently, he focuses on platform engineering and observability, building the culture and tools needed for high-performing teams and reliable systems.

Software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Oli Lane: A few years back, I have this really vivid memory of a customer complaint coming in. It was late on a Friday, of course, they always are. I was just letting my mind wander towards the pub, and this message comes through. It's a big customer, it's a customer we need to keep happy. They said, my backup job ran like an hour late, what's going on? They were pretty annoyed, rightly so, they need to trust that our backup product works, and it's solid and it's dependable. Of course, we dug in. We had our dashboards. We had our metrics. We had our logs. We had our alerts. We did some rooting around, we came up with some plausible theories. We put in a few fixes, a few improvements to make sure that any of the things that we suspected it was wouldn't happen again. I got to the pub a bit late, end of story.

There was this thing that didn't sit right with me and it was that we never really figured out the most important question, which was, why did that job run late and why was it late that time? It was like a murder mystery with the last chapter ripped out. It really annoyed me. This talk is the story of getting from there, where we're squinting at graphs and making a good guess, but mostly shrugging to being able to point and explain the exact bottleneck in a distributed asynchronous system.

I'm Oli. I'm an engineering team lead at Gearset. I've worn many hats, but recently I've been focused on levelling up our observability and our incident response and our team culture as well so that we can build reliable, dependable software, especially as we scale.

Julian Wreford: I'm Julian. I've been part of Oli's team for the last three years as we've built out those observability tools and recently stepped into the team lead role for the team that Oli's been leading.

Oli Lane: From this talk, we're hoping you'll take away a practical knowledge of how to better understand the performance characteristics of your queues in particular, and we'll go through the foundations of OpenTelemetry and build on that to explain practical strategies that we've used to turn our queues from that point of confusion within our teams to something that we really feel confident running in production. We'll discuss different strategies to measure queue health, and then we'll finish off with some tips and tricks that we really wish someone had told us when we were getting started. You should go away better equipped to understand why metrics and logs aren't enough to truly understand your async workflows and how OpenTelemetry might help, how to know when your queue is healthy or unhealthy. How to empower your teams to measure and debug how customers are experiencing your system, and how to take that next step and get your teams adopting this stuff.

Let's take a step back for a minute. Why do we need queues in the first place? Your system probably doesn't start with a queue right from day one. If you've got queues, you probably added them after hitting either a pain point or to resolve some architectural problem. For us, we started with all our code in a single monolith, looked a bit like that. We had multiple replicas of that monolith but only one image that actually shipped. At some point, we needed to organize that better and we decided to split off a few things to handle different responsibilities. Specifically, we wanted our scheduling code, so that was the code that was responsible for kicking off user jobs at specific times. We wanted that to run separately from our core application code. We did that in the simplest way possible. We spun up a new service, it had its own database.

To begin with, it would just poke a HTTP endpoint on the core app and it would kick off a job. Simple enough. That was a good start, but it had some immediate problems and some of these might feel familiar. We had no ability to smooth the load. We had a whole load of customer workloads configured on the scheduler, and one of those workloads was backups, and we let people pick when they wanted to run their backup. I don't know if you've ever given people a date, time picker for their backups but almost everyone picks midnight. Unfortunately, that meant that at midnight, our scheduler would suddenly DoS our application code with hundreds of requests to start some really heavy jobs in parallel. When you synchronously call via HTTP from one service to another and you expect a response, you still, in some ways, have a hard dependency between those services. Dequeue rate, how many are being taken off per time period. Then the in-flight count, which is just how many are currently being processed. The basic idea here is if your enqueue rate is consistently higher than your dequeue rate, you're putting more into the bucket than you're taking out, and the queue size is going to grow. One thing we noticed was that all of these queues weren't created equal. There were some queues where we were fine with the delay. Actually, once we did install the collector, we saw some immediate benefits. The real power of the collector is in its configurability. It has a reliable core, but then a huge array of plug-and-play components, which you can very easily plug into your telemetry pipeline. It can ingest almost any type of telemetry you can think of, transform it, and emit it as OTel or any other format you're choosing. The really powerful part of this is that you can fuse disparate telemetry signals and integrate them into the telemetry coming out of your main components.

For example, we have our collector set up to collect various information about the Kubernetes pods the telemetry is coming out of, such as pod names, image versions, IP addresses, and a whole host of other useful pieces of metadata that means we can correlate when we're doing the querying. This data is then attached to all of the trace data that our components generate, without any of our components having to collect and attach those attributes themselves. You can also arbitrarily transform the data coming through or filter it. We found this really useful for adding an extra redundant layer of defense that scans for any data we never want to see in our telemetry, such as tokens and secrets, and for sending subsets of our telemetry data to different backends for different purposes. For example, some of our workloads now make use of LLMs, and we were able to segregate the telemetry and send it to a different backend because it's useful to analyze it in different ways.

Having one place where we can make these changes rather than updating each of our components separately is absolutely fantastic for our workflows. Finally, from a security perspective, the collector can deal with things like API keys for your observability backend, batching, retries, leaving all of that complexity out of your components. We saw a real uptick in the reliability from offloading this job to the collectors rather than trying to do it in the components themselves.

Thirdly, on our tips and tricks, is another problem we came up against, which is, it turns out some of our traces are humongous, like so ridiculously big they can't really just be looked at manually. Some of our workloads are very large. Some of our longest jobs take days in duration and generate hundreds of thousands of spans. It's all very well generating beautifully connected traces that you can scroll through. If they're too large to work with, everything just becomes unwieldy again. You're back to square one. We did some work to optimize these traces and make sure we're actually omitting things that were useful. Ultimately, at some point, we realized that most of these spans were useful to understand it if we could have it in the right shape. We made use of a different feature that was part of OpenTelemetry, which is span links. Essentially, these are hyperlinks between spans, and they can cross traces.

Honeycomb renders them a bit like this. What we did was that we identified useful subtrees within the wider days-long job and split them up into multiple different traces. In the route trace, we had a single span that represents the whole subtask. Then there's a link to see the trace that represents what that subtask is. Then we can jump back in the opposite direction as well. In effect, it lets us zoom in and zoom out at the trace level, meaning that we have a high-level view of how well the operation took. Then we can jump into different chunks of the operation, even if it has thousands of spans that we need to look at and understand. This ended up working really well for us. It lets us tune out the noise when all we need is the high-level structure, while also being able to dive into the real nitty-gritty detail when we need that as well.

Oli Lane: Something else we've run up against when we've tried to drive adoption across our teams is, how can I jump between all of these tools we now have? Although we've got a lot of gains from pulling all of our observability into OpenTelemetry and Honeycomb, that doesn't mean our other tools went away. We still have logs. We still have time series metrics in Grafana. We still have separate error reporting. We still have some homegrown tools for inspecting product-specific data in a few places. In an ideal world, perhaps, everything would be on a single pane of glass, but in reality, different tools do a better job with different types of data, and different teams also have different requirements from that data that they need to work with. One thing we've really tried to do is link up those disparate data sources. For example, we added the current trace ID to all of our logs in place of a correlation ID.

Then we added links in both directions so that we can quickly switch between views of a trace and views of all the logs generated during that trace, even though we'd use different providers to store those telemetry signals. On the OTel side, that just required generating a hyperlink to attach to each span. In the other direction, it actually required us to write a little browser extension to inject a link into the log UI. We have similar affordances for jumping straight from a trace to the Grafana dashboard for the resources being used by the particular Kubernetes pod we're running on. Lots of other little examples like that where putting in a little bit of work upfront to reduce those frictions has really paid off in terms of the developer experience much more than you might have expected.

That leads into my final point here. We built and integrated all this telemetry as a team. We knew the value that it brought in trying to debug production instance and keep track of our systems day-to-day. In getting other teams to adopt it, we had to meet them where they were at. We didn't come in and say that tracing was this panacea that solves all of your problems. Instead, we worked with them to make it as easy as possible to integrate their existing workflows with this new tech. We ran workshops. We found out their pain points, and we tried to address them. We made sure that when we saw people struggling with something that we thought our new tools could solve, we jumped in and showed them how they could save some time. We also made sure to spread good ideas between team to team, because lots of the teams thought of use cases that we would never have considered.

A lot of this felt like an endless task. People really like their comfort zones. Once folks started to see the value, then they started doing the work and they started adding more attributes, more spans, more data, and that flywheel got stronger and stronger, which got more people to see the value. Soon, most teams were using tracing as their primary source of debugging.

What should you take away from this talk? If you aren't using distributed tracing yet, why not? It's a game changer. It will change how you understand and maintain your service, especially in a distributed systems context. Secondly, when you're designing alerts, remember you're measuring a distribution, so you should alert on that whole distribution. When we talk about alerting, we want to be measuring as accurately as possible the actual user experience and not some internal metric or internal service. Then, finally, just an encouragement that making changes like these are as much a cultural problem as a technical problem. Demonstrating the value to those teams across your business is the best way to build buy-in and get those teams invested in supporting their services and build that flywheel.

Participant 1: I was intrigued, especially as I'm working in C# as well, which I think you mentioned that you were, when you were talking about what you actually had to do to get that trace in across your queues, have you built something custom or are you using what's come out of the box with OTel there?

Julian Wreford: For the queuing side, we've used the OTel specification, and the actual middleware we've put into our queuing layer is really quite small. It's like 100 lines. It's like add a couple of extra attributes to every message, read out those attributes on the other end, and that's where the magic is there. It wasn't super complex to do per instance, but we just needed to do it for each one so that our teams got that out of the box so they knew that it was there. For HTTP, it's already there and we're starting to see some queue providers start writing some of that, but the OTel native hasn't come to a bunch of queue providers quite yet.

Participant 2: Are you storing all your traces? If so, how long are you storing the traces? How many weeks are that?

Oli Lane: We have 60 days of retention, and we actually store almost all of our traces. There is a very good reason for that, and that is that we have a lot of very long-running traces and we really do care about almost all of them, which is unfortunate. You can do clever tail sampling. It's called tail sampling where you make a decision at the end of the trace whether this is a trace that you want to keep or not. We find it really hard to do that because our traces are so long, because you might have to wait four hours to even decide whether to send any of the trace data, and so then all of your telemetry is four hours behind and that's not really very useful. If you have much shorter traces, you can do much more intelligent sampling. For us, it's still a little bit difficult, so I think that's one place where we think OpenTelemetry has a bit of room to grow, but our workaround is just spend a bit more money because it's worth it for us.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

#9858. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9857. [$] Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers

Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.

#9855. What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from an ill-conceived phishing simulation to a hacktivist attack on a US government agency.

Phishing tests can be an important part of cybersecurity awareness training. But as the NBA champion New York Knicks recently showed, they can also go awry.

According to a recent report in The Athletic, Madison Square Garden (MSG) Sports, which owns the Knicks, deployed a poorly timed and ill-conceived phishing simulation ahead of its banner-raising ceremony on Oct. 20. MSG Sports sent out emails to employees with offers of free championship rings commemorating the team's historic NBA Finals victory in June.

Team employees often receive championship rings at the start of the following season. However, the emails in this case were part of a phishing simulation, and when employees clicked on the links to select their rings, they were informed they failed the test and had to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. And they didn't get the rings, either.

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: a hacktivist group breached the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and published personnel records for more than 40,000 employees, and it's unclear how the agency was compromised; and a New York Times report claims a NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles; and, sign up for the Dark Reading newsletter!

#9854. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

#9852. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

After Dark Reading ran this story, Livingston County, Mich., the city of Waynesboro, Tenn., and the Alabama legislature have all implemented or begun working on fixes for their DNS vulnerabilities.

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."

This story was updated at 3:05 p.m. ET on Nov. 10 to reflect actions by multiple US government agencies to address their DNS vulnerabilities.

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9851. For the first time, a C++ standard failed to pass the national bodies

Local 'minimal viable product that everyone agrees on' tanks the C++ standard.

It looks like it happened! A historic first, for better or worse.

This is a sign that C++ is (still) struggling with its governance (see a previous article on cultural issues within C++ here). This is a big deal even if you do not care about programming languages. C++ is arguably the most important programming language in existence.

Your computer runs on C or C++. The web browser you are using to read this is written in C++. ~All programming languages depend on C++ (often through LLVM). Likewise, ~all websites with performance requirements (e.g. YouTube) depend on C++, ~all data storage, game engines, finance, etc.

In a world that is drowning in exciting new vulnerabilities in ~all software, the ability of C++ to change and adjust to changing times affects you.

Let’s take a step back and get an overview. The initial source was a post by Robert Seacord on LinkedIn:

In a comment, J. Daniel GarcÃ­a adds: “There were 12 countries that abstained. In several cases because they could not reach to a common position. That is another signal of a contested draft.”

Now, before we get into the facts: This is not a good look for C++.

There have been multiple fights over the future direction of the C++ language, but no C++ standard ever failed to be signed off by the national bodies.

The national body vote is considered to be a formality. By the time the vote reaches the national bodies all disagreements should’ve been sorted out by WG21 (Working Group 21, i.e. the C++ Standards Committee).

Truly controversial features should never make it this far, since they should never be added to the C++26 working draft in the first place. This is a sign of division in the C++ community, in some form or another, and completely independently of whether you agree with this result or not.

Here, “Added to the C++26 working draft” is essentially accepting the pull request. Everyone is working towards the C++26 release, and people contribute to it with papers. Papers lead to votes, which then lead to amendments of the draft. Finally (this is where we are) wording passes happen, and it gets signed off, rubber-stamped and released. Phrased like this, the ISO process sounds sensible enough, but trust me, it’s actually kind of a nightmare.

Needless to say, the debates are raging, with comments on all sides: So many discussions.

Quick explanation: The national bodies execute a single vote. To pass the national bodies, the draft has to meet two bars:

If the above posts are correct, then the draft failed to meet both bars. Twelve isn’t two-thirds of twenty, and nine is more than a quarter. Visualization:

In total, there were 20 P-members, and 22 total members (ignoring abstaining). I heard that the US abstained, but take that with a grain of salt.

tl;dr: WG21 voted to include Contracts in C++26. Several high-ranking members of WG21 are strongly opposed to Contracts, and so are several national bodies. The national body vote was the ’last resort’ place to prevent Contracts from being canonicalized as part of the C++ standard.

New keywords that replace assert macros with a standardized way to enforce runtime checks. Most importantly, you can add pre and post checks to ensure that all arguments and return values fulfill certain conditions.

Looks simple, right? You’d think so, but no!

First, due to issues with virtual functions, Contracts for virtual functions were already cut from the proposal.

Second, it’s not entirely obvious how this will interact with constexpr or function inlining.

Third, there are compile flags to selectively enable or disable the enforcement. E.g. “If a contract is violated, do you want to 1) kill the program, 2) call a ‘contract-violation handler’ and then kill the program, 3) log an error, 4) ignore completely (and not even perform the check, for performance reasons)?”

Big question: You compile your code with enforce and are linking a prebuilt library that pulls in the same dependency as you, but with Contracts set to ignore. This is fine according to Contracts. The linker gets to keep one of the copies. What happens? Do Contracts run or not? What if a call is inlined across translation units?

Is there even a way for the user to guarantee that checks always run? (The answer is no. What? You were hoping that this feature could be used to ensure certain checks guarding against Undefined Behavior would always run, no matter what? Don’t be silly—this is C++.)

Oh, did I mention that code inside of predicates is just standard C++, so the compiler is allowed to elide checks due to Undefined Behavior?

But do feel free to take it from the source: The “Contracts paper” can be found here, and if you read closely, you’ll find some funny statements that really ruffled some feathers:

It is ill-formed, no diagnostic required (IFNDR) if multiple first declarations for the same function are in different translation units that do not have the same sequence of function contract specifiers.

All of this leads to so many funny issues, some of which can be poorly summarized as “Well, who even knows whether your Contracts are even going to be enforced, this is C++, the compiler can do whatever it wants lol”.

If you think “Gee, this proposal looks rather complex and messy”, keep in mind that the Contracts paper was explicitly designed to be a minimal viable product that everyone would be able to agree on.

If you only faintly paid attention to C++, you might be going into this assuming that Profiles (aka Bjarne Stroustrup’s initiative to make C++ safer via magical fairy dust, also controversial and considered to be ‘impossible to implement’ by some) are the sticking point, but no, Profiles did not make it into C++26.

Oh, y’know, it’s just because that’s all everyone has been talking about.

Most obviously, the pro-Contracts camp released “Do not remove Contracts from C++26” on Oct 23rd, i.e. around the time when the national body ballot closed. Vinnie Falco (the most outspoken voice against Contracts) countered with “Do Remove Contracts From C++26” on the very same day1.

If you’ve been paying attention, there’s a whole trail of papers and events here.

We’ve got talks, and Bjarne Stroustrup, the creator of C++ himself, saying “it’s claimed to be a minimum viable product. It is not minimal. I don’t think it’s viable”.

We’ve got multiple papers, say “Contract Concerns”, “Contracts make C++ less safe — full stop!”, or “Contracts’ fundamental flaws” (all reasonably short) opposing the behemoth that’s the Contracts paper and its rationale document (put together, almost 300 pages).

We’ve had multiple votes. Most importantly (Hagenberg, Feb 15th, 2025), the vote to formally add Contracts to the C++26 working draft, turned out 100 in favor, 14 opposed, 12 abstain. The multiple votes to remove Contracts from the draft all failed, most recently in Croydon, which is also when an amendment to support a mechanism to ensure mandatory contract enforcement failed.

If your eyes are glazing over at this point, I don’t blame you!

The whole situation is a mess, and trying to keep track of it from the outside is a fool’s errand: You’re basically forced to track dry meeting notes, and read between the lines looking at the various drafts people are publishing. Don’t do it.

This is not Contracts’ first rodeo: A different version of Contracts was up for debate around 2018, and was kicked out not too long after. At this point SG21 (‘Study Group 21’) was formed, dedicated to revamping the Contracts concept to get us the new “Minimum Viable Product” that’s currently part of the draft.

The whole situation went back and forth, resulted in fourteen revisions on the Contracts paper, many comments from the national bodies during the process, and finally in some people explicitly calling for the national bodies to veto C++26. (We call that ’the nuclear option’. FYI, some of the people signing this are themselves sitting on national bodies.)

What you need to understand is that the Hagenberg vote (on adding Contracts to the working draft) was strongly in favor of Contracts. 100 in favor vs. 14 against is not a weak result. This makes it incredibly puzzling that this final vote failed so badly (12 for, 8 against is bad).

One narrative on what happened is the following:

“There’s a loud minority strongly opposing Contracts in C++26. This group includes people with a lot of influence, e.g. Bjarne Stroustrup. Some members of this group actively lobbied the national bodies to vote against Contracts, even though WG21 achieved alignment, and agrees that Contracts should ship in their current form.”

This agrees with the evidence we’ve seen (votes in favor, some people strongly opposed). Herb Sutter is suggesting this in his latest paper, see here. (Herb Sutter, for the record, was the chair of the C++ Committee and is (next to Bjarne) perhaps the second-most-important person anyone in the C++ world listens to.)

This is plausible, but I don’t believe it. Not entirely, anyway. Yes, lobbying happened, and Bjarne’s opinion is something people listen to. It’s possible it was the deciding factor, but if it was the deciding factor, then this is a sign that the process itself is broken, and puts undue value onto status.

Even Herb Sutter acknowledges that Contracts were contentious. In footnote 4 on his paper, anyway.

Some of the NBs that voted Disapprove had participated and had expressed concerns about contracts without having to be lobbied (importantly, those were the first-ever Disapprove votes on any C++ DIS).

In other words, before any lobbying happened we already had a historical first, the strongest ever NB disagreement with a draft.

Importantly, it looks to me as though the committee just repeatedly ignored the comments/feedback of the national bodies throughout the process, and then ran face-first into a wall at the vote.

If you think “Oh, you are saying that the committee is just straight-up incompetent and/or evil, then?” No, not really. The committee process is just such a mess that it semi-naturally leads to situations like this. The people working within this system have become so used to the process that they’re barely capable of seeing it.

(Over the years many people who did not find this process workable just left entirely. There’s a huge selection bias effect.)

Part of what makes the process bad is that it’s very “all or nothing”, and the process is so slow that working on the standard is painful for everyone. More on that later.

Anyway. I don’t believe that it’s all just the lobbying. The discussions were already way underway. Evidence:

Taking a look at “Do not remove Contracts from C++26”, it refers to the “23 NB comments on contract assertions”.

Taking a closer look at N5028 and N5031, we see the committee rejected at least one strong anti-Contracts comment from each of the following countries: Sweden, Spain, the United States, France, Romania, the Czech Republic and Finland.

These comments included multiple asks to not ship Contracts in their current form at all, resolve safety issues, make Contracts reliably non-ignorable, fix the const issues, and change it such that standard library hardening phrasing does not depend on Contracts.

What did the committee think? That all of these asks were completely irrelevant? Yeah, no shit people are going to vote against something or abstain if you ignore their concerns.

This was preventable! People told you ahead of time that they were strongly opposed! The national bodies played their part correctly here. They gave you feedback ahead of time, and then voted accordingly.

There were at least four comments asking specifically “Please do not make the work on ‘standard library hardening’ depend on the inclusion of Contracts into C++26.” As it stands, this coupling is still there, i.e. the comments were ignored.

In fact, now that the future of Contracts is shaky, the “Do not remove Contracts” paper includes the following line:

At the time of writing, there is no wording for removing contract assertions from C++26, and producing it is not a purely mechanical exercise. It would require:

removing or respecifying C++26 standard-library hardening [P3471R4], which is written in terms of contract assertions and has never had complete, reviewed wording that is independent of contract assertions.

The audacity. The national bodies were very explicit in saying that they do not want standard library hardening to depend on Contracts.

You went and ignored those comments, and are now complaining about the effort that would be necessary to walk things back? You were given all the heads-up you needed, you just ignored it!

I quote Footnote 6 from Herb Sutter’s paper on the situation we are in. If there is an expert, it is him:

P3911 is the only technical proposal that NBs told us during CD comment processing would likely prevent multiple potential NB negative votes. Itâs also a pure extension that doesnât disturb the rest of the contracts design or interfere with future extensions, which makes it low-cost and low-risk to adopt. This is why in Kona I repeatedly encouraged EWG to pursue it. It addresses what several experts said was their principal concern motivated by safety issues: to provide a way to write a contract in source code that would be guaranteed to be enforced at execution time regardless of build mode or linking. However, it failed to be approved in the EWG 2026-01 telecon (âencourage more work in this directionâ failed by 8-25 for-against, with 9 neutral). Now we have the new information that NBs have rejected the DIS, and several have again cited safety as a critical issue, so this change is likely to increase NB consensus.

P3911 is the paper that proposes adding a way to ensure Contracts will always run, and can be enforced.

(Which, yes, a lot of people believe is necessary for a safety feature. If you can’t guarantee the safety is even enforced, what’s the point?)

Honestly, probably not. Herb Sutter is looking at the situaation from the political angle, and analyzing whose beliefs have more weight based on their status.

Bjarne Stroustrup’s beliefs (as the creator of C++) hold a lot of weight. This is correct.

Quoting Herb Sutter’s discussion on the matter:

Over half of the NBs that voted Disapprove on the C++26 DIS had never participated in WG21 at all and/or never before expressed any concern about contracts in C++26 (most sent no comments on the C++26 CD comment ballot; one sent contracts-unrelated CD comments), yet voted against the DIS after being lobbied with messages citing Bjarneâs opposition.

“Look! It’s just Bjarne having a lot of status!” he says, and he is completely right in saying so, but he is also acting as though putting huge pressure on members to “disagree and commit :-)” hadn’t always been part of it. The C++ Standards Committee always voted in terms of factions.

It was always a political mess where Bjarne’s explicit support was absolutely critical, and where “I know you may disagree with this, but you should vote in favor to get it in” was a part of the process.

Quoting Herb Sutter and Bjarne, yet again from Herb Sutter’s paper:

(Ed.: Bjarne added, when reviewing this paper, that one reason previous DIS ballots were unanimous was his private and public encouragement.)

Why are Contracts authors so obsessed with getting Contracts into C++26? Why not wait for the next release?

Well, C++ has this funny “release train model” (also known as “the frame rule bus stop analogy” in Super Mario Bros. speedrunning). A new version of the C++ standard releases every three years. If your work gets voted into the standard in time, it becomes part of it. If it doesn’t, you have to wait another three years for the next release.

Three years is a long time, and it’s an especially long time to work on a single C++ feature. Getting a C++ paper accepted into the standard is a process so notoriously draining that ~all of the “C++ people” I know just stopped bothering, and stopped working with WG21. It’s bad.

If Contracts don’t get in this cycle, there’s a good chance they never will. They will be nitpicked over the next three years, endlessly litigated, and frankly, I think there’s a good chance several of the people working on Contracts just won’t want to deal with that, and might instead drop out of the process entirely, leaving Contracts dead and buried.

Until the process itself changes, which, god knows how that could happen considering the requirements presumably imposed by ISO, it’s hard to imagine this changing.

This is why the pro-Contracts side released the following statement in their paper:

If the DIS ballot has failed, we should seek another ballot without altering contract assertions or removing them from C++26;

In other words, they are playing a game of Chicken: “We believe you are going to give up first.”

They know full well that a failed C++26 will hurt everyone. But, because the WG21 process is so insane that a loss here risks killing Contracts entirely, and would require another three years of endless litigation and fights, the stakes are high.

As far as I know, the next scheduled WG21 meeting runs Nov 16â21, 2026 in BÃºzios. So, you might think “Ah, then it’s just a few days and they’ll sit down and sort things out, right?”

Well, probably not. The WG21 + ISO process is slow and messy. Even if everyone agrees on whether Contracts should/should not go in, each ballot is open for multiple weeks. So yeah, this may take another year or so.

If C++26 fails, I’ll pour one out. Not for you, but for the many, many people who tried to make you better, and failed3.

If you've made it this far, consider signing up for e-mail notifications, following along on Substack, or adding this blog to your RSS reader.

It’d be slightly easier to take Vinnie’s paper seriously if it didn’t contain Claude-isms like “The ‘purely additive’ claim turns the deferral into a dismissal” that make my eyes glaze over. There has been an uptick in AI usage within WG21, and not all of it has been responsible. ↩︎

Okay fine, there were some tiny concessions, P3878R1 decoupled parts of standard-library hardening from Contract observe mechanics. Still coupled to Contracts though, making it impossible to allow standard-library hardening to enter without Contracts getting in. In other words, the ‘standard-library hardening’ draft was written with the assumption that Contracts would definitely go in. ↩︎

This, for the record, will include the Contracts people (assuming Contracts fail). I am not a big fan of Contracts (for reasons unrelated to any of the discussion here), but I understand the case for them, and the people working on them are (like everyone else) victims of the process. ↩︎

It turns out that some issues people have with async Rust are just downstream of hard concurrency problems.

Companies suck for different reasons. Don't conflate all of big tech into one blob, reason over companies according to their income streams.
