#9799. How do you actually self-host securely?

I recognize that the title is rather vague, but I'm completely green when it comes to self-hosting, so I figured here would be a good place to ask for some pointers given the discussions I sometimes see happening in the comments. I tried researching first through DDG and Google, but (and I recognize this might be a skill issue) most things I found are either SEO slop or trying to sell/market some service.

For some more context and to give a concrete example as to what I'm interested in, I got my hands on a Raspberry Pi which I'd like to use to start tinkering with self-hosting. My main goal would be to host my (static) website on it, potentially adding more things in the future.

Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting, so I'm curious whether it's viable to do it using open source tooling, any gotchas one might encounter, and generally any thoughts you might have on the topic.

(Also, feel free to suggest a tag other than devops, I figured security doesn't quite apply since it's a question and not a write-up/resource regarding security.)

It sounds like what you may want is "nobody can read my packets but me!" If that's the case I would look at the chain of things.

These three are super intertwined, "self hosting" is choosing which of these you want to own.

You may end up using nginx or haproxy somewhere to get ports to line up. But you can also use iptables. Dealer's choice.

Tailscale and Cloudflare tunnels are really cool. They take a bit of the headache away, but you're right that they give up that bit of security (and the learning!).

I'm so psyched for you :) let me know how it goes!

I just drove across the Untied States with my backup MX. My phone provided a hotspot, a GL.inet did tethering and provided Internet, and my backup MX ran a tinc tunnel to give itself a public IP.

Since my backup MX runs off of 5 volts (USB powered) and has a battery backup, I ran it off of the cigarette lighter USB power adapter, but it could've just as easily been off my solar panel (which I run through the hatchback window :)

I always picture it baking in the sun on the cracked back dash of a 1996 Toyota Camry flying down the highway.

I have to admit that I smiled at this too.

I'm not sure if acme.sh is the best choice.

Also, for a lot of self-hosting setups (where you've got a server at home with services that you want to reach from other devices), I'd argue that Tailscale is overkill. Plain Wireguard is pleasantly simple to configure.

Sure, it has some niceties - it has NAT traversal, it's smart enough to figure out more efficient routing than the star topology you'd probably end up with in the simplest plain wg setup, it has fancy multiple user support - but do you actually need any of that?

The reason (the only reason!) I'm using Tailscale instead of WireGuard is that Tailscale has native apps all over the place (including critically for Apple TV and Google's streamer-du-jour), whereas WireGuard doesn't.[1]. Given I don't have to pay anything to use Tailscale, that makes it worth it for me for at least that specific use-case.

[1]: Well, there's a paid subscription app for the Apple TV, and I could jailbreak the Google thing, but there's a limit to how much effort I wanna put into just getting my Jellyfin files available.

WireGuard is available on tvOS. Plain, free, open source WireGuard.

Oh awesome! I'll have to take another look. That was extremely not true in 2024 or '25

Uhhh I was so certain and yet… I think I hallucinated this. Doesn’t seem available.

I'd argue that Tailscale is overkill. Plain Wireguard is pleasantly simple to configure.

I keep hearing this, but I haven't seen anyone explain how to make this work nicely, and all of my forays into wg have been exercises in frustration (not that Tailscale has been pain-free). Getting the tunnel up and running works fine, but figuring out how to keep the tunnel from falling over or silently not forwarding traffic has been considerably more difficult.

Also, I'm not really sure how I would get wireguard working on my Apple TV without Tailscale.

use your pi to ssh to the box you rent, port forward 443 to your pi

When I tried this, the SSH tunnel would fall over all the time and need to be recreated. Seems like at a minimum you need some control loop to watch it, but even then sometimes the failure wasn't "the SSH process went away" but rather that it was alive but silently not working, and I couldn't figure out how to detect this case from the control loop running in the pi so I would have to kick it manually once or twice a month.

In my experience you can get decent reliability with autossh by setting the ServerAliveInterval so that there's always a trickle of traffic. You can also set TCPKeepAlive but since that operates at the TCP level it's subject to middleboxes, which I'd guess is a particular risk on a mobile network.

But I do agree that SSH is not the right tool here.

As a chronic putting stuff publicly accessible online guy, I'd say you get 95% of the way there by:

It's safer to start with services that aren't public facing, e.g. install Tailscale on your phone, laptop, and Raspberry Pi, and then start setting up services you want for yourself.

Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting

I like to do the end-to-end myself but sometimes I just can't be bothered and so use Cloudflare Tunnels to make it work, and that's a better outcome for me than giving up entirely.

I've heard about Tailscale many times but, to be honest, their website reads the same as corporate emails to me, as in I cannot digest any substance from it (might be another skill issue, I know). Would you mind sharing some concrete use case for it (e.g. an example of what you use it for)? That might make it easier for me to grasp the concept.

The simplest way to explain it I think would be to say that Tailscale makes all your devices act like they’re on the same home network, no matter where they actually are.

Their site from 2020 is a bit clearer: https://web.archive.org/web/20201129111934/https://tailscale.com/

But basically it lets your various devices connect to each other, whereever they are, without having to deal with port forwarding, firewalls, dynamic DNS... so your phone or laptop can access self-hosted services on your Raspberry Pi (photos, Jellyfin, RSS, files, ...). It does this while keeping it all hidden from random people/attackers.

I don't use Tailscale, and instead just use plain Wireguard/mTLS, but Tailscale is easiest to set up and seems to be the most popular option for people that want to access their Raspberry Pi when away from home.

I primarily use it for a personal "private intranet"; I host services like Grafana and Forgejo on homelab machines inside my home, and then connect them to Tailscale so I can access them remotely through the tailnet without needing to put them on the public internet. As a bonus it also provides "funnel", a public reverse-proxy which works the same as serving to the tailnet, avoiding the need for a public IP to serve those services.

Unlike traditional VPNs, Tailscale does not tunnel traffic through its infrastructure per se - the control plane server governs access and routing, but traffic transits through establishing point-to-point WireGuard tunnels, with Tailscale operating relays which forward encrypted packets between machines when needed for e.g. NAT traversal. That said, you do give up some amount of self hosting - you can rent a cheap VPS and set up e.g. Headscale to get a decent subset of functionality (though I personally haven't tried this myself).

Tailscale is decent, but if you want to do some learning, I recommend setting up a WireGuard tunnel manually.

My setup is a cloud VPS (on OVH) running TLS termination, which forwards traffic to my homelab server, which connects up to the VPS over WireGuard. That way, my home IP is not publicly visible, and it doesn't matter if it changes or whatever -- my homelab server just reconnects the tunnel and the cloud VPS addresses it by its WireGuard IP.

Specific example: say you want to have a job server whose dashboard you can access via a stable identifier, runs on an isolated machine, and is not exposed to the public internet. Then Tailscale is a great solution. Other examples: tunnels into other VPCs which should not be exposed to the internet; sharing local demos between those in the network; using a specific machine as an exit node when you don’t trust the network you’re currently on; access your devices via stable IDs (eg I have a cluster of Macs whose IPs are dynamic, but I can log in via screen share with stable IDs)

It's simply a way to set up a VPN to your home network. The thing that makes it attractive is that you don't need a static IP for your home to connect to as they do routing through them and it is extremely easy to set up.

But it also means you are trusting them. Personally I do have a static IP at home and my router also supports WireGuard so I am using that. Same thing.

The best high-level overview of why Tailscale came to be, IMO, is https://tailscale.com/blog/two-internets-both-flakey

Ten mentions of Tailscale in this conversation already, I'm going to make it 11.

It really does solve the home lab security problem so well.

Run it on your devices - it works in everything (I even have it on an Apple TV) and it's trivial to install and configure.

Now your phone or laptop, anywhere in the world, can securely talk to the other devices via their 100. IPs (or through Tailscale DNS) - and nothing else can reach them.

And it's free for that kind of personal use!

Prior to Tailscale I was too afraid to even try running a home lab of any sort. Now I have several devices on mine and I actually use them remotely (from my phone) several times a week.

Sometimes I deliberately leave my laptop at home because controlling it from my phone while I'm out and about is more efficient than physically getting it out of my bag.

(Tailscale is basically just a wrapper around Wireguard, so if you want to roll your own you can - I'm not nearly confident enough in my own skills to attempt that for something as security-critical as this myself.)

As an alternative to Tailscale I do the same with ZeroTier, which I think predates it (I actually started doing it with an in-house technology we had at a defunct startup called Lima...)

Here're some broad generalzations that may help you.

First, yes, most of what you find using search engines is poor quality, regurgitated marketing stuff. Sure, you can learn good things from those results, but you'll also learn poor practices at the same time. For instance, most marketed how-tos will tell you to download binary programs or Docker images, which might be OK for learning, but become security issues over time.

One good practice is to learn how to install software via source, or at least using a package manager that's updated often. Docker images are made when the creators feel like it, and often have dependencies baked in that are ancient and may have vulnerabilities. A proper packaging system that's updated often will use the same dependencies for all of your software and will be updated regularly, particularly when any of those dependencies have exploitable vulnerabilities.

Learn about and become comfortable with the Unix permissions model. It's actually quite good, and what some of these marketing people will tell you is wrong: if you use a separate, unprivileged user for each service you host, and one of those users gets compromised, and it can lead to a root escalation, then the issue is that your system isn't updated enough to not allow a root escalation. The number of people who want you to address the symptom and not the problem is huge, and they often advocate for, for instance, Docker or some other thing because it's popular, not because it actually makes sense.

Don't let feature creep win. I host dozens of Wordpress sites for friends and small businesses, and every time PHP gets updated, someone's site ends up not working because they got excited when setting up their site and install a dozen plugins, most which aren't necessary, but which aren't updated and cause their site to stop working with the latest PHP. I've gotten good at disabling plugins without logging in to WP. It's better to only install and use what you really want to use.

Related to that, I recommend installing, playing, getting everything working properly, making notes, then using those notes to reinstall from scratch so you know which steps are superfluous. Your first install might have twenty steps, but once you understand things, the second might have six. Clean is good.

Avoid passwords everywhere you can. Use ssh keys, only allow access to https login pages to certain IPs or IP ranges, if possible, make those links custom if you can, and so on. An OpenCloud login page that people (and bots) don't know is worlds better than a public one that bots will hit constantly.

For anything that does require passwords, don't reuse, don't use simple or basic passwords, and don't let anyone get away with thinking their weak password is "good enough" or that nobody will find the service to try too hard to log in. Assume everything will get tested, including every username, email address and password in every leak, ever.

Don't believe gatekeepers that tell you that you can't, that you shouldn't do certain things. I've taught people who are non-technical to self-host email. If non-technical people can do it, then why should gatekeepers who claim to be technically proficient be believed when they insist that email can't reasonably be self-hosted?

If you find yourself in communities of people who are condescending to you, or who are trying to tell you that a Raspberry Pi isn't a proper server, for instance, then find another community. This community is a good one :)

Oh - get good, durable storage for your Pi, and have fun!

For only a static website? Only allow SSH private keys, no passwords. Run stable versions of stable distros and patch whenever something bad happens. Use nginx. Turn off everything you don't need, and use a firewall to double-check.

Using a VPN to a server elsewhere is useful, but mainly as a way to avoid having to talk a residential ISP into allowing you to serve websites and such. I like Nebula more than Tailscale, it's a bit chonky to set up but works magically well once it's up. Tried Wireguard and it seemed to have real issues with hole-punching.

A very non-concrete advice is simplicity.

When you self-host, you're responsible for security yourself (duh). And maintenance is gonna be a hobby. So scale accordingly: Choose software that doesn't aim to change from under your feet, because that'll make you put off maintenance (this is what some of us like to use the word "stable" to mean). Choose software that's easy to get back into and understand without having to be in the weeds every day. Choose software that'll at least break in obvious ways. Choose software where lots of things have to go wrong for things to break.

How much you need to care about security is entirely dependent on what you host. I would for example greatly invested in security if I self-hosted a public facing file storage or an email server.

I would in general care much less if as you describe I would be hosting a static website on a Raspberry Pi. The risk just isn't that big. It can't cost you a lot of money since it's your own hardware. The worst thing that could happen is that a stranger gains complete control over your Raspberry Pi. They could possibly probe your local network (but not if you put the Rasberry Pi on a subnet), display other information on your website or put your Rasberry Pi to work on something benefitting them (as part of a botnet or crypto mining for example).

I personally wouldn't consider any of those possibilities as great risks. And as a bonus, setting up logging to detect if any of these were happening could be a fun side project.

I avoid exposing my services to the public internet since I am the only user. They are available only via WireGuard. I use plan WireGuard, but solutions like Tailscale or NetBird are fine if you need something else to deal with configuration for you.

On top of that, I still do HTTPs everywhere (using the ACME DNS-01 challenge so I get proper certificates from Let's Encrypt without exposing anything on the public Internet).

Authentication is mostly based on passkeys (I use PocketID for single-sing-on) and I only use SSH keys (backed by secure enclaves whenever possible).

I run my services in NixOS. For my threat model it's okay to run everything on the same machine but to get more workload segregation you could separate the various services across several VMs/micro-VMs.

I described my NAS setup here: https://arne.me/blog/buildlog-nas#security, tl;dr is Tailscale with self-hosted control server, nothing exposed to the internet, HTTPS, encrypted drives.

I think self-hosting a website from your home and self-hosting other things like storage/rss/photos/etc. should be treated as distinct problems with different approaches. Ideally they shouldn't live on the same system even.

Several years ago, I wrote down how I do it, step-by-step. I still use mostly the same approach, though some of the steps have changed over the years. The biggest difference is that now I use tailscale for new things, and and have my reverse proxy connect to the backend over the tailnet. Tailscale is essentially automating the wireguard setup I described in that post, while adding a few nice features around it.

I like having my own reverse proxy VPS. The cheapest possible Linux VPS from whatever provider you want works fine for this. For new VPSes, netcup is my current favorite. (I also use Hetzner, DigitalOcean and Linode for some projects. They are a little easier to navigate than netcup, and all 3 are available for smaller units of time than a month. For things that will be online for a full month or more, though, netcup's pricing is hard to beat. It does make me chuckle that I'm paying in euros for a server I could bike past on the east coast of the US.)

But if you're only hosting things for yourself and for people you trust on your network, you could skip the reverse proxy VPS and just use your wireguard network/tailnet.

Most things I self host are private use anyway. So my home server only gets network access and I use WireGuard to access things remotely.

This of course doesn't apply to a public facing static website. I'd honestly never host those from home network since that also provides people visiting it with too much geo information than I'd like. So for that I'd rent a VPS and keep it as simple as possible. Either nginx with the lets encrypt certbot or caddy which has certificates build in and also supports static websites.

Make sure security updates are automatically applied, make ssh key only and you already have most of your bases covered as far as static hosting goes.

instead of a cloudflare tunnel you could grab a vps, and set up a wireguard tunnel with NAT. I do this for my torrent and DirectConnect clients, so they get public IPs without UPnP/NAT-PMP. I am considering doing same for Jellyfin so it's available outside of tailscale. But I might still require some extra layer, not sure.

I'm lazy and not a good model, so maybe dont do what I do but:

I have WireGuard set up on my OPNsense box so I can VPN into my home network when I'm out. Services I want on the public internet are just open on 443, mostly static sites but a couple of things like Jellyfin. Services I don't want public have a default deny all in my Nginx config with a whitelist for my LAN and Wireguard subnets. I containerize stuff, idk, I figure if some container escape gets discovered then I'm not the biggest target anyway hopefully I have (encrypted) backups at rsync.net in case anything goes down

That's basically the gist. I guess I also keep my nftables fairly locked down on my server and have Crowdsec to block known bad IPs and can detect some things like port scans and block those too + IP-location based blocking on OPNsense to fully block connections from, e.g. China and Russia,

As you can't control upcoming exploits, you want to:

Reducing the access: Some only allow access to these ports: 22 for SSH (if you leave it on standard port, which you will see some people advise to change), 80 (normally never used except to ease SSL setup via Let's encrypt), and 443 (only for services that need to be public). For the services not intended to general public, people would use a VPN or Tailscale, which means only people you allow on the network will be able to access these (it means you will likely need to help your family member and friends to setup Twingate if you want them to access these, and they won't be able to reach your services from any laptop). Some people find the above even too open, and would reduce it further. Everything is behind tailscale (even SSH), and public services leverage Tailscale Funnel. No port is open on your machine, but a tunnel exist between your machine and tailscale infrastructure that expose your websites there. Reducing impact: The public websites can still be vulnerable to zero days (from tailscale funnel or not), so the idea is containing damage. Run your services in a containers is an easy way to limit impact to that service only if things go wrong (and not the whole server).

If you want to go a bit more advanced, I found this blog contains good advice generally:

There are obviously much more you can do: VLAN for your home server, and a lot of permutation for the same idea: wireguard instead of tailscale, iroh instead of tailscale, VM instead of containers, different service users instead of containers, etc.

I run two reverse proxies: one is publicly accessible, and one is only accessible over WireGuard. The public reverse proxy can only communicate with the public services (e.g. website), and the private one can only communicate with the private services (e.g. Immich). The services can only talk to the reverse proxy and aren't exposed in any other way. This is all done using basic Docker networking.

There are a lot of posts about Tailscale already, but I prefer WireGuard. It's trivial to set up, and there's no magic involved. Some serious missteps by Tailscale, such as this incident, and general enshittification concerns make me not want to use it.

I wrote a simple script to manage and distribute my WireGuard configs and deal with the various edge cases my setup has, but you can also just copy your configs to your devices manually. It really isn't as big of a deal as some people make it out to be.

grsecurity + PaX + RBAC rules, possibly using learn feature to build up ruleset

When configuring the grsec kernel, ensure to set up the socket limitation groups, GIDs which cannot open sockets (or flip it to require membership to open sockets "nosocks vs allowsocks")

Audit the system for setuid executables and, creating similar groups, limit access to them to certain users. If users cannot access a vulnerable SUID executable, they cannot exploit it.

Ensure to set sane limits.conf to avoid forkbombs.

Ring fence stuff with UIDs - one user, one service. That way a hacked service can leak its own stuff and not much more.

Don't rely on containers, sandboxes, or magic solutions. Real security is boring. Boring usually works. Docker, firejail, Podman, cgroups, etc all add code on top of the already-running access control and permissions, and in modern times, more code means more bugs.

Things like SEL4 would be perfectly secure on verified hardware, but that says nothing of the applications you build on top of them.

I, uh, am surprised there are people running grsec for self-hosted stuff. I wouldn't have budget to get that.

Lots of great advice here for a "standard" Web server setup. I wanted to mention that there are some less standard approaches, like P2P and overlay networks, which can side-step issues like tunnelling, DNS and HTTPS.

For example, TOR has a feature called "onion services", where any Internet-connected machine can make a port accessible via a .onion address (I used this twenty years ago to run a Wiki from my dorm room; despite knowing very little about networking!)

Static Website hosting is also a pretty good fit for content-addressed storage like IPFS, dat, freenet, etc.

The downside to these approaches is that they're not quite compatible with a standard OS + DNS + Web browser setup. In the best case, that can be avoided via a gateway like Tor2web or an IPFS gateway; but in the worst case it might require installing a particular client in order to access. That might be fine for applications where you just want to connect together machines that you control.

I assume your internet connection has enough bandwidth to sustain a small to moderate website. Self-hosting a publicly facing service is an order of magnitude more dangerous than self-hosting private services such as photo management applications or media servers because of the security implications. On the bright side, static pages can be hosted securely with relatively low effort compared to LAMP stack.

(a) Applying network segmentation is a good start. The RPi should not be able to communicate with other devices through router / firewall configuration. Maybe allow just one device based on IP or MAC address to access the RPi from the LAN.

(b) Then setup DNS records. I assume you own an FQDN. Use an ready-made or custom script to update the DNS records. I'm using dnscontrol alongside envsubst and to perform the changes but there are simpler solutions out there.

(c) Once the DNS is working and updating properly, use an application to issue SSL certificates. My favourite is acme.sh but there are quite a few polished alternatives, e.g. certbot, lego, etc.

(d) Now you're ready to setup a reverse proxy. Note that modern rev-proxies like Caddy can manage (c) on their own. I'm not using them, I'm familiar with nginx so I use that.

(e) Create a deployment user with minimum permissions and use that user to upload data via sftp or other secure protocol. If you want to setup a deployment pipeline via git, that's also possible through webhooks.

(f) Secure the system. I'm pretty sure that you can flat-out ban the big cloud CIDRs. That will save you from dumb scanners abusing your website. Since very few humans use these addresses for outgoing connections, I think it's a good strategy to block them straight-up. You can setup a cron script to download CIDRs and update your firewall "block" tables.

f.1 Make sure you setup some sort of monitoring, so that you can quickly measure things like resources and even incoming requests (e.g. response latency, No of incoming requests, etc). Since you're going to self-host you'll have log access which means full visitors info.

f.2 You might want to explore the possibility of setting a "chroot"

f.3 Alerting: pushover is a good "host -> mobile" alternative, another is to setup the SMTPd in a way that the system can send you emails with status reports, etc. to your personal email.

(g) Backup everything locally (e.g. another NAS) or remotely (backblaze is fairly cheap), or both.

Many people suggest some publicly facing tunnel / proxy server, but doesn't this defeat the purpose of self-hosting: if you are running a VPS proxy, why not just host things on that proxy? If you're using some VPN service, why not just use AWS or something? Self-hosting loses its independence.

Well, conceptually yes, in practice it's a trade-off between security & convenience. If you tunnel to a cloud service the traffic, you still own the data and most of the infra, and just delegating data passing to an external service (I wouldn't rent a whole VPS for that though, and just leverage off-the-shelf solutions like Tailscale or Cloudfare) You can still do the same without these external services (Headscale or Wireguard self hosted, and/or a proxy for the few public facing websites), it's all a trade-off about what you want to manage.

A VPS proxy can be just a gateway into your network, and you don't need much resources for WireGuard. A tiny VPS at $5-12 per year is enough. Your machines at home likely have more resources to host the applications.

To echo the other comments in this thread so far, I've similarly used the Tailscale/Cloudflare Tunnel combination. Tailscale for "personal" services (Syncthing, remote wake-up, etc.) while the Cloudflare tunnel is for anything publicly available (e.g a library site). Yes, definitely less learning than trying to full roll up your own infrastructure, but it's free and fairly painless while giving me a bit more flexibility w.r.t how I'm hosting services.

Anders Pitman had collected a boatload of resources regarding this:

https://github.com/anderspitman/awesome-tunneling

Both closed and open source solutions are listed.

From looking at it just now, it still seems to be actively maintained

Services like cloudflare tunnels have little to do with security. The problem they solve is getting incoming internet traffic to a server without a public IP address. Those are very different problems.

Some ISPs give out fixed public facing IPv4 address. If this is the case, set up port forwarding and enjoy. Otherwise, you'll need a reverse proxy service. Cloudflare tunnels is an option, but it's also easy to run your own on a rented server. (which can also work for non-HTTP services)

In any case, proxy based systems will introduce a dependency on some other server. If you don't like this, go complain to your ISP.

If your router at home is capable to forward a port, do a http port forwarding to your raspberry pi, get your public ip and put it in your dns. Note sure what you mean with security but an exploit on http is pretty small for a static website. If you want more security put your site in docker with a user other than root. Lot of fun, a lot to learn.

One thing I don't see mentioned here is---if you host a web site, your ISP connection will be swamped with bot activity if it's publicly available. There are multiple ways to mitigate this, but they all come with different tradeoffs; Cloudflare is easy to set up, but you are relying upon a huge corporation that is part of the web consolidation problem. The other solution is to tune your web server/firewall to limit concurrent connections/block traffic, but that's more work on your side.

Personally, I do self-host, but it's a VM server that I manage myself. It's not a ton of work, but I do keep an eye on it and have had to spend quite a bit more time than I wanted in tuning Apache (which I've been using for 25+ years) not to fall over (to the point of compiling it myself with a custom module to limit IP connections).

You can start small and (relatively) safe and use CloudFlare to give you free DNS, TLS certs, a Tunnel that'll let you sidestep a lack of static IP (if you don't have such a thing) and put you behind their infrastructure.

You can then take steps towards running your own pieces of that, as you gain confidence.

Making your own TLS certs is pretty easy, using Let's Encrypt, and there's plenty of tooling to run that for you automatically if you just run through its setup process.

Running your own DNS can also be easy, and there's plenty of material to read. If it's a site that you don't mind dropping off the web occasionally if (when) you're waiting for DNS to propagate after you messed up an entry, just do it and enjoy!

Not really an answer to your question, but I think hosting publicly accessible sites for broader access through your home internet is a bad idea, because if you get real traffic going to it, you are likely in violation of your ISP's policies and risk ending up in a bad position in the future. Home internet is how I work, so if I lost it, I would be hurting. You're also opening yourself up to getting your home internet DDOS'd, which would also hurt quite a bit and make your ISP grumpy.

If your site is static, you can host a static site completely for free with Cloudflare R2, and publish it easily via wrangler. No need to expose your home network in any way for a static site, that seems like overkill to me. I understand it's about learning and tinkering and so on, but the amount of learning and tinkering you're going to do while hosting a static site is basically nil. Personally I think there is more learning to be done figuring out how to generate a static site and publish it automatically via wrangler. This is also a great way to run a Wordpress site as you can use Wordpress safely on your home network, use a static site plugin to generate the site, publish it with wrangler, and avoid all the 'hacking' attempts that come from having a Wordpress site.

Personally, I run all of my homelab services inside containers and expose them via Cloudflared, and I know you already dismissed this, but I am not quite sure why as the only thing Cloudflared does is terminate TLS and eliminate issues with residential dynamic IPs. Other solutions for handling this are just as automated these days (caddy, nginx+certbot, etc), there's little difference and not much learning to do there.

I think ~mw and ~marginalia have covered most of the advice I would give. The only thing I have to add to that is that for hosting larger amounts of services, NixOS is the only operating system I will use. Its packages (nixpkgs) have good defaults -- most services have extensive sandboxing already set up for you -- and it provides for one place where all the vulnerability-knobs (i.e. open ports, weird user permissions, etc) can be found. It also forces you to be very explicit about security. If there are any services / dependencies with critical CVEs, it will refuse to build until you enter their names and versions verbatium into the configuration file. This is simultaneously good motivation to not run vulnerable software, and also serves to alert you if you missed a vulnerability report.

Though for hosting smaller amounts of software, really whatever's fine. I run Alpine Linux with HAProxy on my VPS. Just make sure you understand the system, and update it frequently.

In theory I agree with what most people wrote, but I kinda exactly don't want to expose any machine on the LAN to the internet, not even just by port forwarding https.

Maybe one day I'll make a local VM that has no connectivity to the lan so a potential attacker would need to break out of that VM first.

Plus the problems with DNS and addressing hosts from the LAN and from outside, but maybe I have not read the tailscale docs 100% correctly.

Used to have my apps exposed to the internet for ease of access but following the stream of AI hacks, got Tailscale and it turned out really way to setup and use. There’s also an open source version called Headscale that you can self host. My apps reside on a Pi I have under my desk and also a free Oracle VM.

#9797. People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 22: You can love AI without being blind to cybersecurity being sacrificed for utility.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello everyone, and welcome back to Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I am so excited to introduce our guest, Jaya Baloo, who is currently CISO and COO of Aisle. Welcome. Thank you so much for joining us, Jaya.

Jaya Baloo: Thank you so much for inviting me, Becky. Thank you.

DR's Becky Bracken: We are thrilled you're here. I want to explain to our audience a little bit about why I am so particularly excited to have you here. Recently, I was in the audience at ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, and Jaya gave what I just thought was a blockbuster talk about sort of merging AI and quantum, and it was fascinating. There's a specific chunk of her talk that I invited her to talk about today. And it's something I'm just calling: Why is everyone so weird about AI?

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

And so, it stuck with me for days afterward. I kept having the conversation with people because, as I was just explaining to Jaya, we hear people talk about this on the edges, but I hadn't heard a technologist and an expert explain it so plainly, which I think Jaya is also sort of your superpower. But just in the past couple of days, we have Sam Altman who came out saying no one needs their own RAM. They're calling him "RAM Altman." I mean, it's just that people are weird. So, can you explain to me why you dropped that section in, and do you know why it stuck with me for so long? Why is it hitting so close?

Jaya Baloo: I think it's because for ages, when we looked at AI, we had this notion of the uncanny valley, you know? Like, at what point is it so convincing to me that I think I'm speaking to a human? And I think it's clear to say we've passed this uncanny valley. We're fully, you know, believing the conversations that we're having with AI. They could be coming from another human. So, the tendency for us to anthropomorphize the conversations, the interactions that we're having with AI is growing and growing.

And you see people who are not just having a sort of delusional psychosis sometimes of aggrandizement of their own intellect when talking to AI and convinced because of some of the sick fancy that's built into AI that they're super intelligent or their ideas are incredibly unique and creative, or that they're actually the ones to save humanity. You know, I think that the problems that we see with people who are potentially susceptible to that are just made much worse by the current evolution and this current state of AI that we have today. It's just so real. It's so convincing. And we then tend to make it more human.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

DR's Becky Bracken: So, let's go through some of the examples that you gave in your talk. One of them that made me cackle out loud was when you were playing video of a robot doing kung fu with a caption: Why can't we teach it to do laundry? Explain that example for us.

Jaya Baloo: Yeah, so really what I'm talking about is that, you know, we already have a whole bunch of threats right now when we're dealing with AI. And that's really about AI's capability to both uncover vulnerabilities as well as having vulnerabilities in and of itself. So, AI as a potential for insider threat. As we already have these problems, both in our legacy tech debt and in the new technology that we're building with AI, we have more problems.

Now, I have no idea who thought this was a great idea to take these things that are entrenched with these problems, and put it into something that can actually cause physical harm and teach a robot, which by the way, I should be clear, this was the Unitree humanoid robot. It was announced a little bit over a week ago. But let's say that it was announced at the end of October. And this robot was demonstrated on YouTube to do all this cool kung fu stuff.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

And the issue with this that I have is that this can cause actual physical harm. What is it actually bringing humans in terms of value? And honestly, I would be much happier with a humanoid robot that can do the wash, fold the laundry, and sort it out in the kid's hamper. That would be helpful. It wouldn't be something where I'd be terrified to have this thing anywhere near us. And I think that this is something that I feel is genuinely problematic. Just because you can doesn't mean you should when it comes to some of these implementations. And if you cannot get the security right, don't exacerbate and increase the potential for doing damage and harm to humans.

I feel like we forgot that as we're building. You know, we need to solve tech debt, we need to make sure that we have secure-by-default systems, and then you can implement it in something that coexists with us in the physical realm. So that was my point about that. But I really want to say the real issue here is that Unitree had not one, but two, remote backdoors in its quadruped robots. There are multiple security issues with its humanoid robots. And I think knowing that you can remotely take over these robots, and again, like they're capable of physical harm, I think that we really need to rethink and really considerately position these types of devices in light of things like the Cyber Resilience Act.

You know, should we allow hardware and software manufacturers to bring out this kind of technology with the potential risk that it poses? And not just from a cyber perspective, but from a physical one as well.

DR's Becky Bracken: What were some of your other top examples of what's another one that you'd like to highlight here of people being kind of weird about AI?

Jaya Baloo: Well, so I think a slide that you may have initially seen is, and I kind of didn't want to reference it right away in my first answer, was about the fact that we're getting strained in terms of the religiousness around AI. That we both have this tendency to first say, actually, you know, maybe they're sentient, which Anthropic has been talking about in the Vatican with different religious leaders trying to talk about the potential consciousness of AI.

And although I love science fiction, I love it, I just feel, are we really there yet? Are we there, or is this a marketing ploy? What is this? And I'm genuinely trying to understand because it polemicizes what should be a very rational debate into two camps. Those who believe, like already now, we're at the point of talking about consciousness and sentience of these AI systems.

And then the other camp, which actually rebukes AI in the name of Jesus. And I think that was the slide that people also laughed at the conference about. But this is real. And I find it bizarre that we have these phenomena happening and that we don't fully understand the societal consequences either of introducing these systems, which again, let's talk about what they are. They're a bunch of graphics cards in a data center running software.

I am a full Kool-Aid drinker of the notion of complexity and emergence and understanding that even though with a relative set of simple ingredients you have potentially complex outcomes. Drank that Kool-Aid long ago. I believe in this stuff, but I just don't think we're there yet.

So, I feel this has a sort of reductionism effect for the debate that we should be having over how do we do responsible AI by pulling it into these two polemic camps.

DR's Becky Bracken: You also tied it to a lot of end-of-times cult-like thinking, but it does raise the question, which you sort of alluded to a moment ago, how much of this is being driven by marketing of these frontier models, of the [Sam] Altmans of the world, of the Peter Thiels of the world who are out talking. How much of a receptive audience are they finding in the cybersecurity sector, do you think? I mean, is that the primary dynamic at play?

Jaya Baloo: Well, look, I think that we need to separate what is actually happening, which is we do have a bunch of vulnerability discoveries that are happening because of AI. We do have automation for real. It is genuinely happening. We do have automation of these hacking frameworks from Strix, RTec-Ai, Cairn. We are seeing hacking frameworks that are actually in RTec specifically, that are actually being used in real-world hacks. So I'm not trying to discount the facts.

However, what I'm urging to do is the call that, for example, Ciaran Martin, the former head of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), always makes, which is, "Calm the FUD down."

And the fear, uncertainty, doubt that we're introducing here is not helpful. And the reason that I find it really unhelpful is because we know to a large extent how we should perform some sort of containment in terms of egress filtering and sandboxing of these systems.

They may not be perfect, but we've always worked with this notion of defense in depth: assume that one measure fails and that you have additional countermeasures to prevent an actual collapse of the security of the system. I think that that is something that we are actually forgetting right now. And I think it's really important to say, OK, what are the things we genuinely need that would be considered helpful innovation for this? And I think that what we're missing is a lot of the observability here around these AI systems.

So, for example, if we're trying to understand how these systems have potentially been poisoned or Trojanized inherently, then the ability to actually understand how that training data has been populated, even when you only have open-weight models, that would be helpful.

Another thing is additional understanding around this notion of J-space (Jacobian space). So, agent intent. If you know that you have a human operator that brings their own intent to the mix, you know and understand that an AI system might have capabilities and intent that diverge from that human operator, you need to understand when and where that first point of evidence for collecting that divergence could be. We're not there yet either.

So, I would like us to focus on those things rather than the FUD, like Ciaran Martin and a bunch of other renowned cybersecurity people have been saying for a while, like we really need to focus on the things that are breaking.

And really need to focus on the things that we need to be building rather than everyone up in arms about this "Vulnpocalypse," "Breachpocalypse," etc. Apocalypses that are predicted.

DR's Becky Bracken: What is the best way to push back against this sort of rampant anthropomorphization of these agents? You know, I mean, even when researchers are using words like they will "cheat," which assumes that there is a moral compass there to begin with. But at the same time, the goal is for them to be as human as possible? How do we thread that needle?

Jaya Baloo: "They will cheat" is the reward hacking notion that this is a utility that is trying to find the shortest path to success. That means that things that a human would consider part of that moral compass, not to cheat, not to lie, not to evade, etc., that we are projecting this somehow on these AI systems and assuming that the guardrails that we've put in place will cover it.

But I don't think that you can make that assumption clearly, because I don't think we're always in the position to inspect all of the guardrails and know when they've been appropriately applied. And so, I think that there's also this issue of finiteness. Can you have a finite set of guardrails that are actually encompassing the kinds of things that you want to do? And I think the answer to that is probably not.

You know, you’re probably still going to have a few things that escape your potential for, like having this perfectly constructed set of guardrails. Those are like mathematical limitations.

What I would love to encourage us to do is genuinely try to understand better the types of technology that we put into our networks, give access to our data, give a single API token and say "YOLO" to our enterprises, because I don't think we have this under control. And I think that's the real worry that I have.

If we don't understand fully and we're not aware of all of the potential risks, for example, cheating or lying, misrepresentation, etc., if we don't understand that, then we certainly can't have all of these elevated privileges and permissions that we're doing. I think this was the point I was trying to make about when you have capability, you need to kind of always have this subset of this accountability and authorization that you're giving something. And right now, we forgot that lesson. You know, we said, here's all the stuff that you've got access to. You go. And I really feel like we need to rewind a little bit just this part. And that requires better understanding of what they're capable of in terms of the risks.

DR's Becky Bracken: So, what is the next step forward? If you had your team and you were seeing some of this sort of extreme thinking, you know, seeping into your defense planning, what would you say to them? What is the correct reset function here?

Jaya Baloo: I'm really worried about the fact that we are genuinely at risk of losing some of the critical thinking when we're applying AI systems. And you see that already with our coding practices; we are allowing more and more of that initial thinking. So, planning our projects, actually executing the code, reviewing that code, proving it, etc.

DR's Becky Bracken: Which is shocking in such an evidence-based field. You know, it is shocking that it's gone so fast. Am I right?

Jaya Baloo: I feel like we kind of learned this lesson in security in the past too. So it's kind of like, Back to the Future, as well. Every time we tell people about "you should do this because it's secure," if it's not an easy or fun thing to do, you know people won't do it, right? The utility surpasses the convenience. All of the brain elements that would constitute your frontal lobe warning you for this risk. Like, we just lose it. We become teenagers again. Our risk level and tolerance are high. We are happy to take these risks if it makes our life a little bit easier. And I think we shouldn't forget that.

So, AI as an assistant is an incredibly powerful, incredibly useful tool. And especially when we're trying to drive efficiencies with all this technology and all this cost. And you're talking about, you know, "RAM Altman." I think the accessibility of AI and the sovereignty of it is not something we should be taking for granted. And it absolutely is a problem.

So, knowing all of this, you know, the drive to get this convenience, to get this utility, to get this thing available, that is so overcoming any type of hesitation we would have, like, "Is this safe? Should I really use this?" "Will I get dumber if I keep doing this all the time and outsource my thinking?" And I think that's where we actually still need to keep in mind this notion of: What are we giving up to get this utility?

DR's Becky Bracken: Maybe that's why what you were saying hit so hard because I haven't heard a lot of technologists take that position. You know much better than I do, but they are all gas, no breaks, whatever it takes, let's just not lose the wave. And this return to critical thinking, it seems new. Among your peers and colleagues, do you hear the same kind of concern about losing critical thinking?

Jaya Baloo: I think this is the problem with the Kool-Aid. I think at Aisle we certainly have that. I think there's a strong tendency amongst security professionals, but also AI professionals. So, my co-founder, Stanislav Fort, who is amazing, has always kind of thought about AI safety and interpretability. And he has been the person to say, for example, we initially set up Aisle to do vulnerability remediation. And you can imagine that as a CISO, I was like, all right, if we can do this and we can do this well, let's just remediate all the things. Let's just give it access. And he has always urged caution, always urged caution to say, "You know what? We're not there yet"

Unless we can fully confidently trust the AI to make those changes, I always want a human approving the PRs to any code request. I just don't think that what we have in our co-founder is a universal quality in all AI companies. So, I think that like my other co-founder, Ondřej Vlček, who is CISO for multiple companies, including Avast. We have this tendency because we've been burned. So we are, you know, a once-burned, twice-shy kind of notion.

We really think about this from a security-oriented risk-mitigation perspective while actually wanting. I have to be very honest with you, I love AI. But that love shouldn't be blind. It should take the appropriate measure of what is it that I love? And why do I love it? And, you know, what is the benefit to humanity? And Becky, there's a story that I didn't tell on stage.

There are so many good things we can do with AI, but the one thing that I'm the most encouraged of is ... have you heard about the story with the guy and the dog in Australia?

DR's Becky Bracken: No, I don't think I have.

Jaya Baloo: So, this was a machine learning engineer whose dog developed cancer, inoperable, and the dog had to be put down, was the diagnosis. And what he then did is sequence the dog's DNA. You know, this is a guy with no biology background, sequenced the dog's DNA, and figured out what was wrong in the DNA that caused the cancer, developed an mRNA vaccine with AlphaFold.

The most expensive part of the experiment apparently was to actually synthesize the vaccine. And then he administered it to his dog; he had to get permission for that. And Rosie's tumors shrank, and she's is still here and is still hanging out and playing ball with this machine learning engineer.

So I love this story, and this is why I love AI. Because I think if it can unlock the potential benefits, that is amazing. I want those benefits. I just want to make sure that we minimize the downside risks that are inevitable with this kind of technology. And we just need to figure out how we do that. So, we shouldn't go screaming into the abyss, like, yay! You know, I don't want us to be a bunch of lemmings following AI down the abyss.

I just want us to manage that risk and take the benefits while eyes wide open, understanding that right now we need to make sure that we do have enough RAM, you know, and that we do have sovereign compute, that we do not sacrifice all our clean water

DR's Becky Bracken: No one has to give up their computer for OpenAI?

Jaya Baloo: Yeah. I think the future of AI is probably more decentralized than the frontier labs have us think right now.

DR’s Becky Bracken: How much of this is being driven by investment dollars and hyping up stock price? Because we talked around in our editorial meeting about well, is this just a collective psychosis issue? And it's like, well, first, let's be careful about saying "psychosis," but also are we being marketed into a psychosis?

Jaya Baloo: I would love to have a balanced approach. I'm not saying that there's no marketing being done. I think that is certainly being done. I don't think we should eliminate that. I think it would be naive to assume otherwise. At the same time, going full tilt that it's all just marketing is the wrong approach. I think two things can be true at the same time. And I want us to consider this more nuanced thing. And I really want our brains to hold the capacity that both things are true.

There is absolutely a marketing effort. OK, when you have these kinds of companies going to IPO and it's not just OpenAI, it's also Anthropic, and it's also probably a whole bunch of other, you know, parts of this wheel that are actually driving this rage. But there are genuinely risks that we must counter. So, I really do worry about that. And I don't think that that is psychosis.

You must have seen the filing of Anthropic for the IPO. And one of those things that is in that document is there's a very real existential threat that AI could kill us all. I think that's maybe the first time that was ever put into a filing of a company potentially going to IPO. And even there, I think, surely that is not marketing. Surely there are intelligent, thoughtful humans that want to warn of a potential risk that they genuinely see for themselves. I think we need to evaluate the difference between that and how much space there is between the marketing and the genuine risk. But I do think there is a genuine risk. There is. And we shouldn't downplay it as psychosis, while at the same time recognize that there's marketing.

DR's Becky Bracken: I want to thank you so much for coming. You've given me a whole other set of things to think about. Thank you for sharing your deep expertise and your thoughts with us today. We really appreciate it.

Jaya Baloo: No worries, thank you for having me.

DR's Becky Bracken: This has been Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I'm Becky Bracken. Thank you so much for joining us. We'll see you next time.

#9795. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9793. AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Researchers unpacked, mapped, and recreated complex software and the Turla malware, raising opportunities and concerns for organizations and cybersecurity analysts.

Mainstream software and malware can be reverse-engineered more easily than ever, thanks to artificial intelligence (AI) tools — something that security researchers are warning has implications for cyber defense, intellectual property (IP) theft, and beyond.

Household applications typically run on hundreds of thousands, if not millions of lines of code. They incorporate hundreds of third-party libraries, gobs of files, and complex webs of interconnected components. Unpacking and mapping it all is exactly the kind of task that was so difficult before AI, but is now totally in range for even small teams and individuals.

Cybersecurity researchers from Intezer recently tested out how easy it is to reverse-engineer software with AI by picking on some high-profile candidates: Slack, Apple's Finder app, and, importantly for security researchers, the Turla malware. Ironically, the malware proved the most difficult to wrangle. They found it only moderately challenging to meaningfully recreate Apple's and Salesforce's proprietary apps from the ground up.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

"It lowers the bar," Intezer senior security researcher and malware analyst Nicole Fishbein says of AI. "In the past, to reverse-engineer a software, you needed experience. You needed to understand Assembly, and it took a lot of time. Now, I don't want to say anyone [can do it], but it is much easier."

As one would when applying AI to any other major task in cybersecurity, to properly reverse engineer a large program, one needs a "harness." A harness is a little mech suit that focuses a model or models on a specific task, provides it whatever tools it needs to perform its task, and defines its various permissions and restrictions.

No matter her target, Fishbein recalls, "Every case required us to build a different harness, just because the [programs] are so different. For example, if in one case you can just ask Claude to reconstruct the source code, in another case Claude will refuse. Or with malware, when I wanted to be very safe and not execute anything, we had a more complex harness with an extra model."

The malware reconstruction harness ended up consisting of a deterministic Python control plane wrapped around a compiler, with a virtual machine, various static analysis tools, and multiple large language models (LLMs). "We have an Orchestrator agent that controls this whole thing and sends tasks to different sub-agents. It takes the whole binary and breaks it into smaller functions, based on what tools like Binary Ninja provide. From there it goes through a process of reconstruction that is done by one agent, and another agent will test the results," she explains.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

By the end, Fishbein and her colleague built a Turla replicant featuring its full working pipeline: how it receives and executes commands, its file transfer mechanisms, more or less everything. For malware researchers without overly tight deadlines, she says, "If you can recreate the full picture and not miss any key components, that gives you a lot of information."

Fishbein notes, "When we started this research, something that I had in the back of my mind was people that vibe code apps that mimic other very common apps. I was just curious to see how possible it is" to mimic the source material nearly exactly. It didn't turn out to be exceptionally difficult, though results did vary.

The researchers' Finder simulacrum could support plenty of everyday uses as the real app — various file actions, local search, etc. — but the original didn't reveal enough to allow them to mimic its internal structure precisely.

Slack went over more easily. Whereas Finder relied on files managed by cloud services, and actions whose results depended on other macOS services, Slack offered little that the researchers couldn't easily unpack by reverse-engineering its Javascript source code. They reproduced the full client "very simply," they wrote, though they had trouble precisely reconstructing its server, information about which wasn't so readily obtained. It's possible, too, that a real-life attacker interested in stealing Salesforce's proprietary code, or picking it apart for vulnerabilities, might not put too much stock in the infrastructure side of things anyway.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

On Sept. 10, Anthropic released a report describing how threat actors have been abusing its models. Among other cases, it described significant activity from the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, primarily targeting Ukraine's government, military, and diplomatic staff. As part of its campaign in Ukraine, Midnight Blizzard had stolen a complete, proprietary software development kit (SDK) for a drone vision system. Over a period of "several days," with help from Claude, the advanced persistent threat (APT) reverse engineered it. The target was of course unsurprising, given that drones have contributed massively to the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Elsewhere in the same report, Anthropic described a Chinese campaign whose goals included malware development, reconnaissance against foreign governments' networks, vulnerability discovery in major endpoint security products, and more. To manage so many workflows at once, the actors ran Claude in different workstreams, one of which involved reverse-engineering security products in search of bugs.

In addition to nation-states, Fishbein points to evidence of reverse-engineering lower down on the threat actor totem pole. "We see a lot of malware that all of a sudden will become open source. There is a tendency of taking malware that threat actors see works well, and then either leaking the source code, or just recreating it and making it open source to anyone," she says.

And, of course, AI is helping reverse engineering reach the upstanding masses. Last month, an open source (OSS) tool and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server called "REA" — short for "Reverse Engineer Anything" — became the single most popular program listed on GitHub.

Now that reverse-engineering is so much faster and more attainable for more people than ever, vendors may need to take more caution with their IP. Their first step might be to define what outcomes they wish to prevent, before deciding on defensive measures. For instance, reverse engineers can straightforwardly reproduce the Slack client, but even in that case they'll not be able to recreate its entire implementation. "Right now, what the research shows is that as long as you haven't [exposed] your server-side infrastructure to the customer, you're protected," Fishbein notes.

To protect their source code, ironically, developers might take some pages out of hackers' playbooks. Malware developers (and cautious corporations, historically) have long proven the efficacy of effective encryption, obfuscation — perhaps, even, with help from AI — and other anti-analysis measures in frustrating the cybersecurity defenders interested in reverse-engineering their creations.

"Encryptors or different anti-cheating mechanisms that have been around for a while would also help," Fishbein says, "but it is hard to tell how long they will hold, with every new model [getting better] every month."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9791. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9790. AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.

AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.

Research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which was, unbeknownst to users, copying secrets to a hidden file and committing them with the rest of the developer's code.

Among specific secrets leaked were "a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database," Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote in the post.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, "from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors," they wrote.

The issue stems from how coding assistants — Claude Code, in a specific case that the researchers examined — carry out certain commands. "Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file," the researchers explained.

The tool will ask the user before running the command and, if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," then "it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder," according to the report.

"Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code," the researchers explained.

The fact that a routine development task creates a security exposure is dangerous for organizations, especially because these AI coding tools are supposed to be helpful, not harmful, notes Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing for database security firm Liquibase.

“A developer approves a command to save time, the AI agent retains credentials as part of that approval, and those credentials can eventually end up in a public repository," he observes via email. "Nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible."

In the case of Claude Code, Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, finding that 1,122 files contained real secrets. The researchers identified 1,379 distinct secrets in those files alone, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

Claude Code is not being overtly careless; it does try to protect files when it creates its .claude/settings.local.json file inside a Git repository, the researchers noted. The tool does this by adding the file to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore the file on that particular developer's machine. This prevents it from being included in routine commits.

However, the protection is not built into the development project itself, and the "ignore" rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, the researchers noted. "The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it," they wrote.

Moreover, Claude Code itself was sometimes responsible for committing the exposed files. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file.

The action that exposes these secrets while using Claude Code appears to be a "dead zone" of sorts for developers using AI coding assistants, so they likely have no idea that they've just exposed a secret, observes Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

"A 'don't ask again' prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file, and many developers clicking it likely don't know that file exists," he says. "Once it lands in a repository, it sits in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through."

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing the findings. After their publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, said in public comments that although Claude Code historically has not done secrets scrubbing, the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure described by Apiiro, according to Apiiro's report.

Those approaches may be to make sure auto mode catches the exposure, or to build in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas that Anthropic will prototype "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping something with its next version of Claude Code, Cherny said.

Indeed, the leakage exposes how Claude Code's protection relies heavily on a developer-specific Git setting rather than a safeguard built into the project or the AI coding tool itself, exposing a gap that can turn an ordinary command approval into a persistent credential leak.

To avoid this, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held, and open all fields and delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Meanwhile, security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repos, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

"As AI agents become more involved in software development, organizations need to recognize that source code isn't the only thing they need to secure," McCurdy observes. "Agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information, and traditional security checks may not catch everything."

She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze.
