Table 24: Secondary camera-motion activity durations in SDG-SynHuman. Secondary motions are compositional layers that may overlap temporally, therefore reported durations are independent per-motion totals rather than shares of a fixed duration budget.

The dataset is delivered in 1,215 tar shards under shards/, each bundling 200 samples. Per sample (keyed by UUID): RGB as H.264 in video/uuid.mp4; FFV1 lossless 1080p depth in depth/uuid.mkv with a companion JSON recording depth range, resolution, frame rate, and dtype for metric reconstruction; per-frame camera data in meta/uuid_camera.json; scene-level metadata in metas/uuid.json (environment, lighting, agents, camera configuration, animation tasks); and asset-level metadata in description/uuid.json (spawned inventory, motion assets, placements, provenance). All annotations are generated deterministically from the USD scene graph. Fig. 34 shows sample RGB and depth outputs, for both the exterior and interior views.

SDG-Warehouse (PhysicsAI-WorldModel-Synthetic-Warehouse-Operation-Scenes) is a synthetic video dataset of indoor industrial-safety events rendered in fully simulated warehouse environments. Real surveillance footage of these events is rare, hard to release at scale, and seldom carries the kind of dense ground truth that physical-AI training benefits from, so we generate it in simulation, where the event is guaranteed to happen, every parameter is controllable, and every frame is paired with deterministic per-pixel and per-object annotations. The release covers four representative scenarios—a forklift–human near-miss (23%), a warehouse fire with worker evacuation (36%), a forklift–shelf collision (20%), and a warehouse box-pickup action (21%)—totaling ∼123K clips (∼412 hours of video) at 1920×1080 and 30 fps, with multiple synchronized camera viewpoints per simulation run.

All four scenarios are built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Procedural scene composition—warehouse layout, shelf placement, prop variation, and per-light randomization of color temperature, intensity, exposure, and color—is handled by Isaac Sim Replicator Object (IRO). Agent and sensor population—worker spawning and behavior, forklift placement and navigation, and the camera rigs that define the dataset’s multi-view viewpoints—is handled by Isaac Sim Replicator Agent (IRA). Camera placement is parametric, with height, distance, and look-down angle sampled per run, and worker assets and motions are sampled from Isaac Sim’s character library to diversify human appearance and gait. Each simulation run is seeded with a unique random seed that controls all randomized variables (scene composition, lighting, agent identity and motion, camera pose, and event timing), so runs are independent and reproducible.

Each camera viewpoint provides an H.264 RGB clip with synchronized per-frame annotations: metric depth (raw plus log-normalized colorized variant); instance segmentation (per-pixel IDs traceable to specific simulated objects, with a colorized variant); shaded segmentation (3D-aware rendering with normal-based shading); a Canny edge map computed on the shaded segmentation; 2D tight and loose axis-aligned bounding boxes plus 3D oriented bounding boxes for every tracked agent and prop; and per-frame camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Each annotation stream is also released as an encoded video alongside the RGB clip. Run-level structured metadata records scenario type, random seed, asset and agent inventory, event parameters (e.g., forklift dodge distance, fire ignition location, exit waypoints), and lighting randomization. Figure 35 shows the modalities for one frame per scenario.

Figure 35: SDG-Warehouse dataset. Sample view of the four scenarios and the annotations (RGB clips, metric depth, instance segmentation, shaded segmentation, and Canny edge).

Figure 36: Joint embedding geometry of pre-train and SDG. PCA→UMAP projection of 20,000 pre-training cluster centroids (gray) and 200 randomly sampled clips from each SDG source. Each SDG source forms a distinct, tightly clustered region that overlaps only narrowly with the bulk pre-training distribution.

To verify that synthetic content is genuinely complementary to the pre-training corpus, we analyze its position in the Cosmos-Embed1 video embedding space relative to clusters from the pre-training distribution. Fig. 36 visualizes the joint geometry of pre-training and SDG embeddings, while Tab. 25 quantifies the distance from each SDG source to the pre-training manifold using an in-distribution self-reference as a baseline. Together, these results show that SDG occupies long-tail regions of the embedding space that are not sufficiently covered by web-scale pre-training alone.

We study how different synthetic data generation (SDG) sources affect video generation quality and domain understanding by fine-tuning our pre-trained model (Cosmos3-Nano) on each source individually and jointly. We evaluate all variants using PAIBench-G T2V benchmark (Zhou et al., 2025c), which reports an overall score, a perceptual Quality score, and six domain-specific sub-scores: Common Sense, AV (autonomous vehicles), Robot, Industry, Human, and Physics. Results are summarized in Tab. 26.

Table 26: Ablation study on synthetic data generation (SDG) datasets, evaluated on PAIBench-G T2V (Zhou et al., 2025c). Each model is fine-tuned from the same pre-trained baseline with data from one SDG source; SDG-All mixes all five sources. Bold denotes improvement over the baseline; underline marks the best score in each column. Colored deltas show change relative to the baseline (green = improvement, red = degradation).

A consistent pattern across all SDG variants is that each source lifts different domain-specific scores, reflecting the unique content distribution of each simulator. SDG-DriveSim yields the largest gain in the Robot domain (+0.89) and a strong Common Sense improvement (+0.52), reflecting the rich structured dynamics of driving scenarios. SDG-RobotSim improves perceptual Quality most among all sources (+0.26) and moderately lifts the Robot score (+0.23). SDG-Warehouse provides broad positive deltas across Overall, Domain, AV (+0.29), and Physics (+0.21), while maintaining strong in Robot (+0.60). SDG-PhyxSim delivers the largest single-domain gain: a +0.85 uplift in Industry and a +0.80 gain in Robot, driven by its physics-grounded industrial and manipulation content. SDG-SynHuman is the standout individual source, posting the best overall score (79.79) with the highest positive deltas in Domain (+0.29), Common Sense (+0.66), AV (+0.47), and Robot (+1.23). The breadth of human-centric synthetic content appears to provide a strong general-purpose signal that transfers across multiple evaluation domains.

The most consistent pattern of degradation across all SDG sources is the Human domain score, which drops in every single variant without exception—ranging from −0.38 (SDG-SynHuman) to −0.69 (SDG-PhyxSim). Notably, even SDG-SynHuman, which is specifically built from synthetic human-centric scenes, fails to recover this score. This suggests that the sim-to-real gap is particularly pronounced for human-related visual content: current simulators do not yet replicate the subtle appearance, motion, and behavioral nuances of real humans with sufficient fidelity to benefit this evaluation domain. More broadly, domain-specialized sources can also degrade orthogonal categories—SDG-RobotSim hurts AV (−1.03) and Industry (−1.22), while SDG-PhyxSim’s physics emphasis comes with notable AV degradation (−1.42)—underscoring the need to mix sources rather than rely on any single simulator.

Mixing all SDG sources (SDG-All) yields uniformly positive deltas across eight of nine metrics, with only Human showing a residual dip (−0.47), consistent with the sim-to-real gap observed above. It achieves the best Quality score (72.56) and consistent improvements across all other domain categories, demonstrating that data diversity suppresses individual source biases. Based on these results, our final model incorporates the SDG datasets together with real, high-quality videos during a dedicated mid-training stage. This design allows the model to absorb the domain-specific physical understanding encoded in synthetic data while retaining the perceptual fidelity and visual realism it acquired from real footage in pre-training.

Cosmos3-Edge uses a dense 2B backbone trained from scratch. Its training follows a two-stage curriculum: pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning. The pre-training stage is further divided into base pre-training and long-context extension. We use BF16 precision throughout training; optimizer settings are given below.

During base pre-training, we train the 2B Edge backbone from scratch on a total of 15T tokens from the Nemotron pre-training corpus, using a sequence length of 8,192 tokens. This stage consists of two sub-stages: general pre-training on a broad-coverage data mixture, followed by continued pre-training on a higher-quality mixture. The data mixture is hot-swapped during training: continued pre-training resumes from the general-pre-training checkpoint while preserving the optimizer state and learning-rate schedule, so only the data mixture changes. We use AdamW with peak learning rate 1.2×10−3, (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at norm 1.0. We use a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule, aligning the data-mixture switch with the transition from the stable phase to the decay phase. The tokenizer is shared with the NVIDIA Nemotron-3 models (NVIDIA, 2025f).

During the long-context extension phase, we extend the context window of the Cosmos3-Edge backbone to 128K tokens. Although the extended context window supports 128K-token training sequences, the primary goal of this stage is to improve robustness and quality at the deployed 32K-token sequence length. During the context extension phase, we train on 128K sequence length with an increased RoPE base of 1e8. We use a constant learning rate of 1.2×10−5 and the long-context phase is trained with 90B tokens. For the data blend in this phase, we downsample the pre-training blend to 80% and add long document QA data as the remaining 20% in the blend.

We use the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data from Nemotron-Cascade-2 (Yang et al., 2026b), which covers a broad set of domains including mathematics, coding, science, general chat, instruction following, tool use, and code-agent tasks. In total, the dataset contains approximately 26M SFT samples. We pack these examples into sequences of up to 128K tokens, yielding roughly 2.6M packed training samples. The model is trained in a single SFT stage with a global batch size of 32. We use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 2×10−5 and (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.98). Empirically, model capability peaks after approximately 1.7 epochs, corresponding to 140K training steps.

We evaluate our SFT model on a set of text benchmarks spanning reasoning, science, instruction following, long context, and general capabilities: HMMT25 Feb (Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament, 2025), GPQA (Rein et al., 2023), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024d), AA-LCR (Artificial Analysis Team, 2025), IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025a), and Scale AI Multi-Challenge (Sirdeshmukh et al., 2025). We compare against Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026b), a strong baseline with the same model size.

As shown in Tab. 27, our text SFT model substantially outperforms Qwen3.5-2B on math reasoning and science benchmarks, such as HMMT25 Feb and GPQA. It yields comparable results on instruction-following and long-context evaluations, including IFBench and AA-LCR. However, it lags behind Qwen3.5-2B on general-domain benchmarks such as MMLU-Pro.

Table 27: Text benchmark results. Comparing Cosmos3-Edge and Qwen3.5-2B across reasoning, science, instruction-following, and long-context evaluations. Cosmos3-Edge substantially improves mathematical and scientific reasoning capability on HMMT25 Feb and GPQA, while achieving comparable scores on IFBench and AA-LCR.

While the main experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Cosmos 3 across a wide range of understanding and generation tasks, they do not fully isolate the contributions of individual design choices. To better understand the factors underlying the model’s capabilities, we conduct a series of ablation studies examining key architectural, data, and training decisions. These studies investigate how the Reasoner and Generator interact within the Mixture-of-Transformers framework, the impact of multimodal training signals such as audio and action data, the effectiveness of temporal conditioning mechanisms, and the transferability of learned world and action representations across domains. Together, these analyses provide deeper insight into the design principles that enable Cosmos 3 to function as a unified omnimodal world model for Physical AI.s

In this study, we investigate how the Reasoner benefits the Generator model. We train two models using the Cosmos3-Nano architecture: one with Qwen3-VL-8B as the understanding tower, and the other with our Cosmos3-Nano Reasoner. In both cases, the Generator tower is trained from scratch. For this ablation, we restrict training to 256p and 480p resolutions with clip lengths of 0–200 frames, and set the sequence length to 25K. Following our large-scale run, we use joint image–video training. Both models are trained for 90K iterations on 256 GPUs. We report PAIBench scores for both below.

Table 28: Understanding tower ablation. We report domain and quality scores on PAIBench T2V and I2V for two variants that differ only in the pretrained model used to initialize the understanding tower while the Generator tower is trained from scratch: (1) Cosmos 3 Reasoner and (2) Qwen3-VL. Subject and background consistency are I2V-specific and not applicable to T2V. Initializing the understanding tower from the Cosmos3 Reasoner yields better domain scores on Physical AI domains than the Qwen3-VL variant.

As shown in Table 28, replacing Qwen3-VL-8B with our Cosmos3-Nano Reasoner in the understanding tower yields consistent improvements in domain scores, particularly in Physical AI domains. On T2V, the Reasoner improves the overall Domain score from 73.7 to 75.7, with the largest gains concentrated in physically-grounded categories: Robot (+4.8, 66.5 → 71.3), Physics (+0.5, 88.7 → 89.2), AV (+2.3, 52.6 → 54.9), and Industry (+1.0, 77.4 → 78.4). A similar pattern holds on I2V, where the Domain score rises from 80.0 to 80.8, driven by gains in Common sense (+0.7), Industry (+0.8), Human (+1.0), and Physics (+0.2). These results suggest that the reasoner provides better embeddings for Physical AI domains for generator to learn. The quality scores for both models are comparable.

We study two complementary mechanisms for conditioning generation on a target frame rate: (i) MRoPE FPS modulation, which scales the temporal axis of the unified 3D MRoPE by the target FPS, and (ii) Text Control, which injects the target duration and FPS as natural-language text inside the structured JSON caption. For this ablation, we restrict training to 256p and 480p resolutions with clip lengths of 0–200 frames, and set the sequence length to 25K. Following our large-scale run, we use joint image–video training. We train 4 models for 130K iterations on 128 GPUs each, varying only whether each mechanism is active: Base (no control), Text Control (text only), MRoPE FPS Modulation (MRoPE only), and Text Control + MRoPE FPS Modulation (both). We curate an evaluation set with known source duration and FPS, ∼100 videos each of 10, 15, 24, 30 FPS (±2 FPS tolerance). We use the structured captions of these evaluation set videos as prompts and generate samples across 3 seeds per prompt at 480p (16:9) resolution. We produce a 5 s clip for each prompt.

We score each clip on Video Quality (VQ; DOVER perceptual quality score (Wu et al., 2023a)) and Dynamic Degree (DD; motion presence on a 0–1 scale (Huang et al., 2024)). From the three-seed DD scores per prompt (p), we compute a normalized motion control (MC) term

MC indicates the robustness of the control mechanism, \ie, the degree of variability per prompt for each control setting. We combine these into a Motion Fidelity score

where DDref is the per-band mean DD over the real-video reference set. The final Composite Score is the product of Video Quality and Motion Fidelity, reflecting adherence to motion magnitude without impacting the perceptual quality of generated videos. This is computed as \mathbb{E}_{\text{FPS-band}}\!\left[(\text{VQ})\cdot\text{MF}\right], computed per FPS band and then averaged across bands.

Tab. 29 reports averages across the four FPS bands. Both mechanisms improve over Base individually; MRoPE FPS modulation alone yields a larger gain than the Text Control (+1.12 vs. +0.77 in composite). Combining the two produces the best composite score (+1.30 over Base). VQ stays within a 0.2-point window across all four settings, indicating that the gains are concentrated in motion fidelity rather than video perceptual quality, \ie, the controls primarily improve temporal behavior. Based on these results, we adopt the Text Control + MRoPE FPS Modulation configuration for Cosmos 3 Generator.

Table 29: FPS control ablation on Cosmos3-Nano. Scores are averaged across four FPS bands (10, 15, 24, 30). VQ is the DOVER video quality score; MF is motion fidelity (0–1); Composite =\mathbb{E}_{\text{band}}[(\text{VQ})\cdot\text{MF}]. Bold indicates best in the column. Text Control + MRoPE FPS Modulation is the most performant control setting that demonstrates adherence to reference FPS band motion while preserving perceptual quality.

We investigate the impact of including audio during continued pre-training on video metrics. Starting from the same pre-trained checkpoint, we train two Cosmos3-Nano variants on our pre-training dataset: one with video-only data and one with joint video-audio data. These ablations are run for 20k iterations on 128 GPUs. We restrict training to 256p and 480p resolutions.

Table 30: Effect of introducing audio data during pre-training. We report PAIBench T2V and I2V scores after continued pre-training of two generator variants that differ only in whether audio is used during training. The video data is shared across both experiments.

The results in Tab. 30 show that continued training without audio leads to a drop in both T2V and I2V scores, suggesting that joint video-audio pre-training does not degrade video generation quality and may provide a modest benefit even when evaluated purely on video-centric metrics.

As described in Sec. 2.2.2 and summarized in Fig. 4, Cosmos 3 supports three action generation modes: forward dynamics (FD), inverse dynamics (ID), and joint video-action prediction (policy). We ablate whether a single joint action model can share useful structure across these modes. We use the PushT dataset and Cosmos3-Edge for this experiment. The model is trained for three single-mode action checkpoints for 2K steps each against one joint FD/ID/policy checkpoint trained for 6K steps, so that each mode is trained for the same amount of optimization steps. We report the PSNR for FD and MSE for ID. For policy mode, we report the policy coverage ratio of the T block and target region aggregated across 50 different initializations, with 10 rollouts from each starting point. The results are summarized in Tab. 31.

Table 31: PushT action-mode synergy. We compare single-mode FD, ID, and policy checkpoints trained for 2K steps each against one joint FD/ID/policy checkpoint trained for 6K steps. Lower is better for ID MSE; higher is better for FD PSNR and policy coverage. Bold indicates the better value in each column.

The joint FD/ID/policy checkpoint improves the action-side metrics while preserving comparable forward-dynamics quality. Compared with the single-mode checkpoints, ID MSE decreases from 1.11×10−3 to 3.09×10−4, a 72% relative reduction, and policy coverage increases from 74.1% to 77.3%. FD PSNR decreases from 27.13 to 26.22, indicating a modest tradeoff in reconstruction fidelity. Overall, the joint checkpoint provides the best policy coverage and ID accuracy under the same per-mode optimization budget, suggesting that the action modes share useful structure even though FD quality benefits slightly from single-mode specialization.

In addition to the closed-loop success rate reported in Sec. 6.2.5, we evaluate how well the video and action streams jointly predicted by Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID remain aligned on RoboLab. Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID is trained only on DROID, so RoboLab provides a held-out environment for testing this video-action consistency. For each predicted action chunk, we execute the same chunk in the RoboLab simulator and compute PSNR between the model-predicted video and the resulting simulator rollout, then aggregate the scores across action chunks for the left and wrist camera views. The left third-person view achieves 23.19 dB, comparable to the PSNR levels achieved by our robotics forward-dynamics models on DROID (Tab. 18). The wrist (eye-in-hand) view is more challenging because the camera moves with the end-effector and the model must infer newly revealed content; nevertheless, it reaches 17.33 dB. These results indicate strong consistency between the predicted actions and predicted videos. Figure 37 visualizes this consistency: the predicted frames closely match the corresponding frames from simulator rollouts initialized from the same state.

Figure 37: Predicted video vs. simulator rollout on RoboLab. For the wrist and left cameras, Sim Env shows the video recorded by executing the predicted action chunk in the RoboLab simulator from the same initial state, while Pred shows the video predicted by Cosmos3-Nano-Policy-DROID jointly with that action chunk. We observe that the predicted video closely matches the simulator rollout.

Cosmos-HumanEval (Cosmos-HUE or HUE) is an evaluation benchmark for video generation introduced in the main results section. HUE provides a human-reference signal via atomic binary questions generated per video by a Vision-Language Model (VLM) pipeline and scored along the four HUE dimensions (Semantic Alignment, Physical Laws, Geometric Reasoning, Visual Integrity). This appendix complements that overview with the formal binary scoring scheme, the annotation protocol and reliability estimates, and the per-dimension and per-domain Text-to-Video (T2V) and Image-to-Video (I2V) leaderboards.

Each Layer 3 question elicits Yes (criterion met), No (clear violation), or Unclear (e.g., the region is occluded or the motion is too fast to assess, or the video fails to depict the event the question presupposes, e.g., the prompt calls for a right turn but the lead vehicle never turns, so the follow-up question about a smooth curved arc has no clear Yes or No). Unclear is treated as No: a model is not rewarded for failing to produce the prompted action, and a non-confident annotator is conservatively counted against the model. Concretely, Unclear does not contribute to the Yes numerator but remains in the denominator, so a video that is mostly Unclear cannot score above one with the same number of explicit Yes answers. Let \mathcal{Q}_{v} denote the set of questions issued for video v; the per-video HUE score is

with HUE⁡(v)∈[0,100]% since “Yes” is always the desirable outcome. Model-level scores aggregate over V test videos:

The grand mean weights every answered (video, question) observation equally, avoiding inflation from videos that happen to receive fewer applicable questions. Dimension-level scores are computed identically by restricting the sums to questions belonging to each dimension.

Each video receives up to 16 atomic binary questions from the three-layer pipeline above, and each (video, question) pair is independently rated by two human annotators. If the two annotators agree, the consensus answer is recorded as the canonical response; if they disagree, the question is escalated to a third quality-control (QC) reviewer, whose answer is final. This double-rating + QC-tiebreaker workflow yields a single canonical answer per (video, question) pair, bounds the contribution of any single annotator, and produces the auditable response stream that the scoring formulas in Equations 12–13 operate on.

Authoring and refining atomic questions targets two goals: low variance (re-running the same model on the same prompts produces a similar score), and GT saturation (real videos paired with the prompts score at or near 100%). We use these criteria to evaluate candidate questions and to iterate the question bank, revising or dropping items that fail any criterion. The process is ongoing: the GT score remains below 100% (Tabs. 32 and 33), so question-bank refinement continues.

The current T2V evaluation pool samples 100 prompts from PAIBench-G, with 5 random-seed generations per prompt and up to 20 questions per video, yielding up to 10,000 binary observations per model checkpoint. Treating each as an independent Bernoulli trial with underlying Yes-rate p=HUE⁡(m)/100, the 95% confidence interval on the model-level HUE score (in percentage points) is \mathrm{HUE}(m)\pm 100\cdot 1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/N} with N the observation count; in practice this gives CI95 widths around ±0.6 points for top-tier scores on the scale of Tab. 32. Atomic binary judgments reduce within-annotator variance compared to Likert-scale grading, where the annotator must integrate multiple observations, weigh them, and map onto an arbitrary scale. Each of these three operations introduces noise. The Real video GT row scores 93.6 on T2V prompts and 94.4 on I2V prompts, reflecting (i) minor residual prompt–video mismatches in the sampled PAIBench-G pairs despite manual review, and (ii) imperfections in the auto-generated question set, where overly strict, ambiguous, or off-target questions can yield No or Unclear on a real video. We treat the gap from GT to 100% as a north-star for ongoing question-bank refinement.

Tab. 32 reports current T2V results across our model panel and the strongest external T2V baselines. Veo-3.1 leads overall (91.3) and Seedance-1.5-Pro is second (90.0); Cosmos3-Super is the best open-source generator at 89.3, ahead of Wan2.2-A14B (88.2) and Cosmos3-Nano (87.6). The per-dimension picture is more favorable to Cosmos3-Super: it is the best open-source model on 9 of 12 axes, and beats every generator, including closed-source, on AV (87.7) and Physics (91.5). The gap from the strongest generator to real video (Real video GT, 93.6) is ∼2.3 points overall, leaving meaningful headroom for the next round.

Tab. 33 reports the parallel I2V evaluation. Veo-3.1 leads overall (89.7), with Cosmos3-Super trailing by only 0.1 points (89.6); Cosmos3-Nano (88.6) edges Wan2.2-A14B (88.4) and Seedance-1.5-Pro (87.6). Cosmos3-Super beats every generator outright on Visual Integrity (94.2), Robotics (91.1), and Miscellaneous (94.8), and ties Veo-3.1 for the lead on Semantic Alignment (both 90.3); Cosmos3-Nano wins AV (87.6) outright; Wan2.2-A14B wins Physics (91.9). The full I2V slate spans ∼9 points across generators.

#9776. 7 Free Websites Every Content Creator Needs to Know

Do you have the desire to become a content creator, but not have the money to start? Here are 7 free websites every content creator needs to know.

1.Exploding Topics (Trending Topics)

(Photo Credit:- Exploding Topics)

If you're a content creator, you might be wondering what better way to find new topic ideas than to see what people are searching for? This tool gives you this data without anyone else's explanation. It provides related hashtags and tips on how to use them effectively in your posts. It's a great tool for anyone who wants to keep up to date with what's most relevant in their niche. You can also see the most popular hashtags by country, making it easier to understand cross-border and demographic trends. This site makes your search for content easier than ever! There are countless ways to use explosive topics to your advantage as a content creator. 

Some examples can be:

  • Use the most popular hashtags and keywords to get inspiration for ideas.
  •  Find out what people are talking about in real-time.
  •  Find new audiences you may not have known were interested in your topic.

There’s no excuse not to try this website — it’s free and easy to use!

Visit Exploding Topics From Here

2. Headline Studio (Headline Grader)

(Photo Credit:-Headline Studio)

Headline Studio allows you to create catchy headlines for your content. After writing a title there is data on how often people view articles with similar titles and why they are involved with them.

This is a valuable tool when creating new blog posts because it generates catchy headlines for your blog post to catch a reader’s attention.

Visit Headline Studio From Here

3. Answer the public

(Photo Credit:- Answer The Public)

Answer The public is an excellent tool for content creators. It gives you insight into what people are asking on social media sites and communities and lets you guess about topics that matter to your audience. Answer the public allows you to enter a keyword or topic related to your niche and it will show results with popular questions and keywords related to your topic. It's an amazing way to get insights into what people are searching online and allows you to identify topics driven by new blog posts or social media content on platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Youtube, and Twitter as well as the types of questions they ask and  also want answers.

Visit Answer The Public From Here


4. Surfer Seo (SEO Ranking)

(Photo Credit:-Surfer Seo)


With this tool, content creators can quickly and easily check the ranking of their websites and those of other competitors. This tool allows you to see how your website compares to others in different categories, including: 

  • Rank Potential
  • Organic Search Ranking

Surfer Seo is free and the interface is very friendly. It's a great tool for anyone who wants to do quick competitor research or check their site's rankings at any time.

Visit SurferSeo From Here

5. Canva (Templates/Graphics)

(Photo Credit:- Canva)


Canva is a free graphic design platform that makes it easy to create invitations, business cards, mobile videos, Instagram posts, Instagram stories, flyers, and more with professionally designed templates. You can even upload your photos and drag and drop them into Canva templates. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop. You can also remove background from images with one click.

Canva offers thousands of free, professionally designed templates that can be customized with just a few clicks. Simply upload your photos to Canva, drag them into the template of your choice, and save the file to your computer.

It is free to use for basic use but if you want access to different fonts or more features, then you need to buy a premium plan.

Visit Canva From Here

6. Facebook Audience Insights (Audience Research)

(Photo Credit:- Facebook Audience Insights

Facebook Audience Insights is a powerful tool for content creators when researching their target market. This can help you understand the demographics, interests, and behaviors of your target audience. This information helps determine the direction of your content so that it resonates with them. The most important tools to consider in Facebook Audience Insights are Demographics and Behavior. These two sections provide you with valuable information about your target market, such as their age and from where they belong, how much time they spend on social media per day, what devices they use to access it, etc.

There is another section of Facebook Audits that is very helpful. This will let you know the interests, hobbies, and activities that people in your target market are most interested in. You can use this information to create content for them about things they will be about as opposed to topics they may not be so keen on.

Visit Facebook Audience Insights From Here

7. Pexels (Images)

(Photo Credit: Pixel

Pexels is a warehouse for any content creator with millions of free royalty images who wants to find high-quality images that can be used freely without having to worry about permissions or licensing so you are free to use the photos in your content and also there is no watermark on photos

The only cons are that some photos contain people, and Pexels doesn't allow you to remove people from photos. Search your keyword and download as many as you want!

Visit Pexel From Here


So there you have it. We hope that these specially curated websites will come in handy for content creators and small businesses alike. If you've got a site that should be on this list, let us know! And if you're looking for more content creator resources, then let us know in the comments section below

#9775. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9774. November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:Ivanti ICS Zero-Day Attacks Highlight Vendor Patching Hurdles

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

While the cornucopia of CVEs this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he says via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

Tara Seals is an award-winning journalist with 25+ years of experience as a reporter, analyst, and editor in the cybersecurity, communications, and technology spaces. As managing editor, she runs the newsroom at Dark Reading, leading a team of staff writers and freelance contributors. She also heads up strategy for a variety of in-depth, multichannel news coverage initiatives.

Prior to joining Dark Reading in 2022, Tara was editor-in-chief at cybersecurity stalwart Threatpost, and prior to that, the North American news lead for Infosecurity Magazine. She also spent 13 years working for other titles at Virgo Publishing (now part of Informa TechTarget), as executive editor and editor-in-chief at publications focused on communications service providers, channel partners, and enterprise mobile and video technology. In 2026, she was awarded a regional Azbee award for her in-depth coverage of the ongoing North Korean fake worker cyber campaign.

A Texas native, she holds a B.A. from Columbia University, lives in Western Massachusetts with her family, and is on a never-ending quest for good Mexican food in the Northeast.

#9773. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

#9772. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9771. N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

The RMM provider also released a hotfix as one of recommended mitigations to address public exploits for the alleged zero-days that allow for attacker takeover.

N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers that broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers already are scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates.

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

More recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody says.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he says. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise."

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

Researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or new scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools."

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody says he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

"Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he says. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.
