#9746. Lava Security and OWASP Focus on the Overlooked Risks Behind GPU Cloud Infrastructure

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

The security of an AI workload depends on more than the applications and models running on it. Beneath every deployment sits an extensive infrastructure environment responsible for processing, networking, storing, and managing the data required by artificial intelligence systems.

As GPU cloud capacity becomes increasingly important to organizations running AI workloads, the security of that underlying environment deserves greater attention. Neocloud providers and AI data center operators must account for vulnerabilities involving hardware, firmware, networking technologies, management interfaces, and shared operational systems.

Lava Security is bringing these issues into focus through its Top 10 Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks framework, which has become an official OWASP project.

The initiative was developed by Yakir Kadkoda, CTO and Co-Founder of Lava Security, and Michael Katchinskiy, Head of Security Research. It is designed to help infrastructure providers, operators, and organizations purchasing GPU cloud capacity better understand the security challenges affecting AI environments.

Modern AI data centers combine thousands of GPUs with high-speed networking, specialized management controllers, shared storage, and complex orchestration systems.

Many of these technologies were originally designed for trusted high-performance computing environments. Their growing use in commercial neocloud environments, where unrelated organizations may share physical infrastructure, introduces additional security risks.

Bare-metal neocloud deployments illustrate the issue. Customers may receive root access to rented servers, giving them substantial control over the computing environment. However, if management interfaces are not adequately restricted, that access could allow changes to hardware boot configurations.

Those configurations may persist even after an operating system reinstall. If a server is subsequently reassigned without resetting the affected settings, another customer could inherit a compromised environment.

This is one example of why infrastructure security requires visibility into components that conventional operating system and application protections may not cover.

"AI infrastructure introduces attack surfaces that traditional security approaches may not adequately address. Organizations need to understand what happens below the operating system, particularly when hardware, firmware, and management interfaces are shared across customers," said Michael Katchinskiy, Head of Security Research at Lava Security. "This framework helps make those risks easier to identify and provides practical guidance for addressing them."

The OWASP framework examines vulnerabilities across multiple layers of the infrastructure stack.

Its coverage includes compromised server firmware, weaknesses in high-speed networking technologies such as InfiniBand and RDMA, inadequate tenant isolation, and insecure out-of-band management interfaces.

It also considers supply chain threats, data center facility systems, shared storage and AI artifacts, incomplete security certifications, centralized operational services, and delays in vulnerability patching.

These categories are intended to provide a broader picture of how infrastructure vulnerabilities can affect an entire environment.

Each category includes potential attack scenarios, real-world implications, and practical mitigation recommendations. Infrastructure providers and operators can use this material to evaluate their environments and prioritize security improvements.

For organizations purchasing GPU cloud capacity, the framework also offers a reference for understanding the controls protecting their workloads.

According to Lava Security, it initially published the framework in July 2026. Its development drew on disclosed vulnerabilities, incident reports, technical documentation, and the company's research into AI infrastructure security.

More than 20 security and infrastructure practitioners also provided feedback during its development. Their backgrounds included neocloud providers, hardware OEMs, security companies, universities, and research institutions.

The framework's transition to OWASP gives the initiative a structure for continued collaboration, allowing contributors from different parts of the infrastructure ecosystem to participate in its evolution.

Kadkoda believes that this broader perspective is essential to addressing the security challenges affecting AI environments.

"Securing AI infrastructure requires looking at the entire environment, not just individual components. Hardware, networking, management systems, and workloads are interconnected, and risks in one area can affect the security of the broader infrastructure," said Yakir Kadkoda, CTO and Co-Founder of Lava Security. "Developing this framework within OWASP gives the community an opportunity to contribute its expertise and continuously improve how these risks are understood and addressed."

The framework will continue evolving through an open development process on GitHub. Security researchers, infrastructure engineers, hardware vendors, and operators can review its contents, challenge existing assumptions, propose changes, and contribute additional research or mitigation recommendations.

Contributors will receive credit in future releases.

The project is designed to develop alongside the infrastructure itself. New GPU architectures, networking technologies, management systems, and deployment models may introduce additional security considerations that the framework can address through future updates.

Those interested in exploring the initiative can visit the official OWASP project page or access the GitHub repository to participate in its development.

As the infrastructure powering AI continues to evolve, the ability to identify vulnerabilities across the entire technology stack will remain an important consideration for providers and organizations relying on GPU cloud environments. Lava Security's OWASP initiative provides an open foundation for bringing that discussion into a shared industry effort.

#9745. Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

We’re excited to announce a new collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗

With these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.

#9744. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

This PHP flaw is a stark reminder of how much of the web runs on shared infrastructure — one critical bug can take government and business sites offline at once. I have been following the patching updates closely, and TrendWire has been a useful source for keeping up with the fast-moving security news around this story. Hopefully hosts patch quickly before mass exploitation ramps up, as the researchers warn.

The vulnerabilities can hardly be referred to as zero-days. They have been known to The PHP Foundation from 2024 but people decided that other bugs were more urgent.

If you’re on shared hosting, it’s worth opening a ticket and asking which PHP build they’re actually running instead of trusting the control panel: the version shown there isn’t always the one serving requests.
